Une bière brune sans alcool, première innovation de Huyghe chez Het Anker C'est la première grande innovation de Het Anker depuis sa reprise fin 2024 par la brasserie Huyghe. Le CEO Alain De Laet a dévoilé ce nouveau breuvage mardi. "Le marché évolue et le consommateur boit moins. Nous, brasseurs, devons nous adapter", a-t-il expliqué avant de laisser la parole au maître brasseur Bart Meulepas. "Dans les bières blondes ou fruitées sans alcool, on peut facilement compenser la perte de goût par le houblon et les fruits. Pour une bière brune, c'est plus compliqué." Il a fallu un an et demi à Bart et à son équipe pour mettre cette bière au point et trouver, à l'issue d'une recherche assez pointue, les malts spécifiques. Le produit est bien équilibré, pas trop sucré et présente une note légèrement grillée en fin de bouche. La technologie présente à la brasserie Huyghe à Melle (Flandre orientale) a aidé l'équipe de Malines qui ne disposait par exemple pas des installations nécessaires pour la double pasteurisation d'une bière sans alcool. "La collaboration se poursuit et nous pouvons, nous aussi, nous inspirer de ce qui se fait ici à Malines", ajoute Alain De Laet, évoquant notamment le centre de visiteurs de Het Anker qui a attiré l'an dernier 24.000 visiteurs. Outre la brasserie, Het Anker dispose d'une distillerie pour la production de whisky, d'un hôtel et de deux restaurants. Quelque 80 personnes travaillent sur place pour 40.000 hectolitres de bière brassés chaque année. Huyghe de son côté dispose d'un outil lui permettant de produire jusqu'à 450.000 hectolitres. "Il est temps de penser un peu plus à l'aspect commercial", poursuit Alain De Laet, précisant que depuis la reprise, la Gouden Carolus Classic était désormais disponible dans de nombreux pays où elle était encore inconnue, aux États-Unis notamment. De nombreuses brasseries ont lancé leur propre bière sans alcool et le marché belge compte actuellement une centaine de références. Mais les brunes sont assez rares. La Leffe est déjà présente depuis 2020, et quelques références étrangères sont également disponibles en Belgique comme La Trappe Nillis ou le stout Guinness La consommation de bière est en chute libre depuis quelques décennies, à l'exception du segment sans alcool. La brasserie Het Anker à Malines en profite donc pour lancer sa première bière du genre. J e vous recommande ce bordeaux intense qui apportera la structure nécessaire pour équilibrer la puissance de votre plat. » C’est une sommelière très particulière qui répond à notre demande d’accord mets-vin pour un steak frites au poivre. Babette est en effet la nouvelle intelligence artificielle spécialisée en œnologie qu’a lancée Colruyt Group au début de ce mois. Elle accompagne désormais les clients de BOIR, la plateforme en ligne du distributeur consacrée aux vins, aux bières, aux spiritueux et aux alternatives sans alcool. Babette ne se contente pas de filtrer les 2.000 références disponibles. Elle prend également en compte les échanges avec les utilisateurs pour affiner ses recommandations, en fonction de leurs goûts, de leurs attentes et de leur budget. « Les filtres traditionnels peuvent s’avérer trop stricts pour cibler l’offre », explique Jeroen Van Belleghem, en charge de BOIR. « L’objectif est aussi de rendre l’univers des boissons plus inclusif, notamment grâce aux alternatives sans alcool. » À lire aussi Le caddie est-il vraiment toujours plus cher ? (infographies) Le responsable de BOIR insiste : « Babette ne remplace pas les professionnels. Elle est conçue comme un complément et non comme un substitut. Nos sommeliers enrichissent sans cesse sa base de connaissances. Le savoir-faire des spécialistes a ainsi été transformé en données structurées et exploitables par l’outil en ligne. Et si notre IA ne parvient pas à répondre à un utilisateur, elle le redirige vers notre service client, qui fait alors appel à nos sommeliers pour des recommandations spécifiques. » Pas au détriment de l’humain L’intelligence artificielle va-t-elle bouleverser le métier de sommelier ? « Je comprends qu’une IA puisse aider les personnes lorsqu’elles effectuent leurs achats au quotidien. Mais elle ne remplacera pas l’expertise d’un caviste passionné », répond Hugo Terache, sommelier au restaurant gastronomique Pré de chez vous, à Bouge. Il se montre même réservé : « Je crains que certains consommateurs ne privilégient l’IA au détriment des conseils d’un sommelier qui teste ses produits. A mes yeux, le vin, comme tout produit de bouche, possède une dimension vivante qui gagne à être découverte à travers un échange humain. L’IA s’appuie sur des avis existants, là où le professionnel mobilise sa propre expérience de dégustation. » Le sommelier précise : « Lorsque je réalise mes accords, j’ai besoin de m’appuyer sur des saveurs que j’ai moi-même expérimentées. Cela m’aide à me projeter dans mes futures associations. » À lire aussi Shopping assisté par l’IA : les Belges avancent avec prudence Reste à savoir pourquoi Colruyt Group a trouvé opportun de lancer Babette… « L’intérêt d’un tel outil réside surtout dans sa capacité à simplifier le choix du consommateur », estime Sandra Rothenberger, professeure de marketing à la Solvay Brussels School (ULB). « Face à une offre toujours plus vaste, certains clients peuvent rapidement se sentir perdus. L’IA pourrait renforcer cette évolution en devenant un véritable assistant à la décision d’achat. C’est probablement là que se situe la vraie valeur marketing de ce type d’outil. » À lire aussi L’avenir enivrant des vins sans alcool Les distributeurs l’ont bien compris, à une époque où le commerce en ligne de biens de grande consommation tend à progresser en parts de marché et où l’IA évolue au galop. Colruyt Group a donné naissance à Babette avant le lancement d’autres projets encore confidentiels à ce stade. Le mois dernier, c’est Carrefour qui avait lancé le bal belge de l’IA au service du client de supermarché avec la possibilité de remplir son caddie virtuel en compagnie de ChatGPT. La prochaine étape pourrait être l’automatisation partielle des courses grâce à l’avènement de l’intelligence artificielle agentique. Mais probablement pas avant la fin de cette décennie. Babette conseille désormais les clients sur la plateforme BOIR, dédiée aux boissons avec et sans alcool. Une IA pour personnaliser et accélérer le conseil à la consommation. Moroccan intelligence accused of spying on journalists and human rights activists. Farmers unite worldwide against what they call ‘chemical colonisation’. Farmers and activists around the world are mobilising on Saturday for an international day of action against pesticides – denouncing products sold by major agrochemical companies that they say are damaging their health and destroying their livelihoods.

France pledges more support to fight DRC Ebola outbreak as deaths top 4,000. France will step up its support for efforts to control Ebola in eastern Democratic Republic of ​Congo, Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Saturday during ‌a visit to a region hit by the virus. The outbreak has killed more than 4,000 people, Congolese authorities said, as they struggle to contain what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

Cry for help as French-Swiss lake dries up in record summer heat. The picturesque Lac des Brenets between France and Switzerland has dried up after a record-breaking hot summer, leaving locals crying out for help to save the lake.

Reintroduction of vultures to France causes friction with farmers. Future of French far-right hope Bardella in balance after antisemitism claims. Rwandan genocide hunter Dafroza Gauthier dies after long battle for justice. Dafroza Gauthier, who spent spent decades tracking down Rwandans in France accused of involvement in the 1994 genocide, has died from cancer at the age of 72. By filing a string of civil lawsuits against suspected fugitives, she and her husband Alain pushed the French legal system to hold them to account.

France struggles to fund farm climate adaptation as losses mount. Farmers in France are expecting their first payments shortly under the government's billion-euro emergency aid package to support farmers affected by severe summer heatwaves, droughts and wildfires. As the effects of climate change worsen, experts say compensation alone will not be enough to protect French agriculture in the long term.

Ethiopia captures Tigray capital as its regional rivals meet in Egypt. Ethiopian federal forces have regained control of the Tigray rebels' regional capital, local sources said on Sunday, while Ethiopia's regional rivals gathered in Egypt to discuss the risk of a wider war.

The pill: from symbol of women's liberation to subject of growing mistrust. Initially a symbol of liberation, the pill went on to become an almost inevitable part of a woman’s contraceptive journey. But today its use in France is in decline, the drop in popularity fuelled by health warnings, mistrust and a changing attitude towards contraception.

US-German trio win medicine Nobel for work on optogenetics. The Nobel medicine prize was awarded Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work in the field of optogenetics.

Nobel Prize announcements begin, with hopes of a 'less controversial year'. With this year's Nobel Prize winner announcements beginning on Monday, among those experts believe could be in line for the $1.2 million prizes are GLP-1 researchers, a Ukrainian children's rights activist and several female authors. Spain PM calls early election after housing crisis defeat. Study shows extreme poverty and homelessness on the rise in France. Chat group kingpin goes on trial in Paris over online abuse of underage girls. How the U.S. Can Once Again Lead on Human Rights. In the post-Trump era, Washington will need to regain credibility. Pluralism is where it should start.
Russia’s Air War Aims to Bleed Ukraine Dry. Vladimir Putin’s latest plan for victory puts a cease-fire well out of reach.
France’s Catholic Revival Is Fueling Its Far Right. French religiosity is surging—in tandem with political extremism.
Sánchez Calls Snap Elections Over Spain’s Housing Crisis. The vote’s timing makes it a litmus test for progressive politics across Europe.
AI Made the List—but Humans Still Did the Killing. In the film “NAZA,” Israeli soldiers reveal the workings of autonomous warfare.
How Much More Trump Trouble Can Indonesia’s Prabowo Take?. Jakarta’s attempts to align with Washington face a growing backlash at home.

Iran sentences 20-year-old blogger to more than 13 years in prison. Iranian authorities have sentenced 20-year-old blogger Iman Sadeghi, who was arrested in Kashan during the nationwide protests earlier this year, to more than 13 years in prison, according to information obtained by Iran International.

Iran oil exports vanish as regional flows surpass prewar levels. New tanker-tracking data shows that Iran’s new oil exports have effectively ground to a halt, while crude exports from Arab countries in the region surpassed pre-war levels in the final week of September.

Four January protest detainees sentenced to death by Tehran courts. Four men detained during Iran’s nationwide January protests have been sentenced to death by Tehran Revolutionary Courts, HRANA reported Thursday, as rights groups warn of mounting use of capital punishment against protest detainees.

US targets Iran auto, rail and metals sectors in new sanctions blitz. The US Treasury sanctioned Iran’s automotive and rail sectors Thursday, expanding its campaign to some of the country’s largest industrial companies as Washington seeks to choke off Tehran’s sources of revenue with Operation Economic Outcast.

Iran links under scrutiny in separate Flydubai, UK airbase investigations. Iran on Thursday was linked by US and Israeli officials to the Flydubai incident, the second such case after British police opened a probe into possible Tehran involvement in a suspected RAF Fairford plot and arrested a dual UK-Iranian national.

Leaked Kremlin plan undercuts Moscow's claims on ruble-rial trade with Iran. A leaked Russian government roadmap obtained by Fox News put the share of Russia-Iran trade settled in national currencies at 68%, far below Moscow’s public claims that nearly all bilateral trade had shifted to rubles and rials.

Iranian press sees diplomacy alive but narrowing after US response. Tehran media see diplomacy with Washington as increasingly precarious but not yet dead, with the two sides far apart over the sequencing of any deal and the window for compromise appearing to narrow.

Iran's rhetoric against UAE hardens after Netanyahu visit. Iranian officials and media have sharply condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to the UAE, warning Abu Dhabi over its deepening ties with Israel amid renewed tensions over three disputed Persian Gulf islands.

A Mossad spy in Iran: From banking infiltration to nuclear and missile sabotage. A former Mossad agent says he spent years inside one of Iran's best-known telecom businesses, using its banking tricks to fund Israeli operations and deleting a file from a switch near Malard minutes before the 2011 blast that killed the father of Iran's missile program.

Can the Caspian give Iran a way around Hormuz?. With war disrupting Iran’s southern trade routes, Tehran is looking north to the Caspian for alternatives. But the available evidence suggests they cannot replace its crucial oil exports.

Al-Qaeda is Iran's quiet backup if the war turns, expert says. Iran has spent two decades keeping al-Qaeda close as a partner it can deny, and could turn to it if the war with the United States escalates, a counterterrorism expert told Iran International. With Hezbollah and Hamas weakened, she said, it is the card Tehran has left.

Iran’s truck repair hub feels the squeeze as work dries up. Business at one of central Iran’s main heavy-vehicle service hubs has fallen by about 30% from a year earlier, offering a ground-level view of an economy where soaring food prices, a battered currency and weaker freight activity are squeezing workers and small businesses.

Shot in leg, forced into hiding: Iran protester recounts January crackdown. Hamid Kouhsari was carrying a wounded woman on his back through the streets of Gorgan on January 8 when security forces shot him from behind. He spent the next eight months in hiding with his leg untreated, before leaving Iran.

Five killed in roadside attack as violence spreads in southeast Iran. At least five people were reported killed on Friday in an attack near Zahedan in southeastern Iran, as the Revolutionary Guards confirmed a roadside bombing in the area that killed one of its fighters.

Iran court upholds film star’s jail term over post mourning protest victims. An appeals court in Tehran has upheld a one-year prison sentence for renowned actress Elnaz Shakerdoost over an Instagram story mourning people killed during January’s protests, her lawyer said Friday.

As the rial sinks, Iranians seek shelter in almost anything else. Iran’s stock market is breaking records even as the dollar and gold hit new highs, an apparent contradiction that may point to the same dynamic: households and investors scrambling to protect their wealth as the rial weakens and the economic toll of the Iran-US war grows.

Iran denies teachers are quitting despite viral resignation videos. Iran’s Education Ministry dismissed reports of teacher resignations over working conditions and security pressure as a “rumor,” despite numerous videos of teachers announcing departures and a teachers’ council warning of a growing exodus.

Two Iranians charged over foiled plot targeting Manchester Jews. Two Iranian men have been charged over a terrorist plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community that was disrupted before it could be carried out, British police said Friday.

'They shot on sight': Amnesty details 2022 protest killings in Kurdish areas. Iranian security forces shot civilians at close range, pursued fleeing protesters and prevented wounded people from receiving help during the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom uprising in Kurdish cities, according to Amnesty International’s investigation into the crackdown.

Officials trade blame as Iran’s economy sinks deeper. Iran’s worsening economic crisis has opened an increasingly bitter argument over who is responsible, as the government points to outside pressure and market psychology while hardliners accuse Tehran’s own economic officials of making the situation worse.

Iran executes man arrested during January protests. Iran has executed Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, who was arrested during January’s protests in Shahrekord, the judiciary’s Mizan news agency announced Saturday.

Islamic Republic's 'slow meltdown' leaves it fewer ways out, analysts say. The Islamic Republic is in a "slow meltdown" that may not bring it down soon but is narrowing its options as the economy sinks, repression deepens and divisions open up among its own hardliners, analysts told Iran International's Eye for Iran podcast.

Smartwatches on Iran's security chiefs spark row within the inner circle. Senior Iranian military and security officials have been photographed wearing smartwatches, drawing fresh criticism of their basic security discipline after years of reports that Israel has used electronic devices around Iranian commanders to track and kill them.

Euro tops 3 million rials as Iran's currency hits fresh record lows. Iran's rial fell to new record lows on Saturday, with the euro crossing 3 million rials for the first time and the US dollar hovering around 2.7 million rials on the open market.

'The end of illness is not treatment. It is death': Iranian MP on the cost of care. Iranians are selling livestock, cars and furniture to pay for treatment their insurance no longer covers, and a member of parliament's health committee says the system has reached the point where falling ill can end in death rather than care.

Khamenei adviser warns UAE as tensions with Tehran escalate. A senior adviser to Iran’s supreme leader issued a pointed warning to the United Arab Emirates on Saturday, saying “imported security has an expiration date” as tensions between Tehran and Abu Dhabi continue to rise.

Iranian women break records and barriers at Asian Games. Iranian women have delivered a record-breaking performance at the 2026 Asian Games, winning medals across an unusually broad range of sports and achieving a series of firsts for the country.

Security meeting, military buildup: US weighs next move on Iran?. An unannounced meeting of President Donald Trump’s senior national security team at Camp David, as another aircraft carrier and thousands more US troops move toward the Middle East, has raised the prospect of another major operation against Iran.

Iran demolishes prison despite warnings of erasing evidence of mass killings. One of the last watchtowers at Iran’s Rajaei Shahr (Gohardasht) prison was demolished Saturday, as authorities dismantle a site of mass political executions despite longstanding warnings that its destruction could erase evidence of crimes against humanity.

Trump weighs Iran decision with ‘all options’ on the table. US President Donald Trump said Saturday he was approaching a decision on Iran, warning Tehran faced the “easy way or the hard way” as the Pentagon kept military options open amid continued attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian currency hits another record low under US economic pressure. Iran’s currency fell to another record low against the dollar on Sunday, extending its decline during a US campaign aimed at restricting the Islamic Republic’s oil exports and financial flows.

Iran reviews US response to seven-day proposal as officials debate next steps. Iran is reviewing Washington’s response to a seven-day proposal sent through intermediaries, a senior foreign ministry official said on Sunday, as other officials offered differing assessments of whether further negotiations with the United States were needed.

Iran’s Olympiad paradox: Building scientific talent for a future abroad. Iran’s scientific Olympiad system has become a pipeline of elite talent into universities feeding sensitive nuclear, missile and technology sectors, even as many of the same high achievers leave the country for better opportunities abroad.

What can Iran’s new oil chief change under the US blockade?. Iran’s oil minister Mohsen Paknejad resigned Sunday, leaving acting minister Hamid Bovard with crude exports choked by a US blockade and scrutiny of intermediaries used to sell sanctioned oil, raising questions over what he can change.

Iran workers face delayed wages, lost benefits and job fears. Workers across several sectors in Iran say employers are delaying or splitting wage payments, cutting benefits and warning staff they could lose their jobs for protesting, as inflation and rising living costs deepen pressure on households.

Iran escalates Starlink threats over fears of losing internet control. Iranian authorities have stepped up warnings against Starlink as the cost-of-living crisis deepens and the prospect of renewed public protests grows, signaling mounting concern over citizens’ access to satellite internet.

Two more January protesters executed in Iran. The Islamic Republic executed two more people detained in connection with the January 2026 protests, bringing to seven the number put to death in the Alikhani Square case in Isfahan, rights groups and the judiciary reported Monday.

Netanyahu predicts Iran regime’s fall, Tehran warns war could engulf region. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu predicted the eventual fall of Iran’s leadership while the Islamic Republic’s top armed forces commander warned a new conflict would engulf the region, sharpening exchanges over the prospect of renewed fighting on Monday.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activate defense pact over Houthi attacks. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activated collective deterrence measures Monday and agreed to rapidly deploy forces and military capabilities to the kingdom, as Saudi-backed Yemeni troops advanced against the Iran-backed Houthis.

Pezeshkian nominates missile-industry veteran as defense minister. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has nominated Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi as defense minister, moving to fill a post left vacant since Defense Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed in US-Israeli strikes in February.

Iran says US talks ‘meaningless’ as third tanker hit near Hormuz. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that talks with the United States were meaningless, even as President Donald Trump remained open to direct negotiations, while a third tanker in two days was struck near the Strait of Hormuz.

IRGC commander says his wife founded Minab school hit in February strike. The school struck in February in Iran’s Minab was founded by the wife of senior IRGC commander Ali Fadavi as part of a wider educational project linked to the Guards’ navy, according to his remarks and an earlier Iranian media account.

IRGC commander, son helped build new oil-sales network. Senior IRGC commander Hossein-Reza Sadeghi and his son Saeed played central roles in efforts to preserve an IRGC Intelligence oil-sales network and shift its financial operations from the United Arab Emirates to Russia, an Iran International investigation found.

Why Iran’s oil minister quit at a critical moment for exports. Iran’s oil minister left office as exports fell sharply and questions mounted over billions of dollars in sanctioned crude sales, bringing disputes over oil intermediaries, corporate management and political pressure into focus.

Iran sentences 38-year-old to death as January protest executions mount. Hadi Abbasian, a 38-year-old resident of northeastern Iran, has been sentenced to death by a Revolutionary Court in Bojnurd after being arrested over his support for the nationwide protests in January, according to information obtained by Iran International.

Iran releases cleric who called for replacing Islamic Republic on bail. Iranian authorities have released hardline cleric Mohammad-Bagher Kharrazi on bail after about a month in detention, the judiciary said on Tuesday.

Clothes, diaries, dolls: Iran forces raid slain protesters’ rooms. Clothes, diaries, books and childhood dolls are being taken from the bedrooms of protesters killed in Iran, as security forces extend pressure on families seeking accountability into the most private spaces of their grief nearly nine months after the January 2026 killings.

Tehran police warn cafes over live music, DJs and hookah. Police in Tehran have warned cafes that they could face closure or lose their licenses for hosting live music, using DJs or serving hookah, extending a broader campaign of enforcement against businesses over entertainment, mandatory hijab rules and support for protests.

Houthi gains reversed at Bab al-Mandab, but Iran’s leverage runs deeper. Saudi-backed Yemeni forces on Monday reversed weeks of Houthi gains around Bab al-Mandab, the strategic strait linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, exposing vulnerabilities in the Iran-backed group even as fighting elsewhere showed how far Yemen remains from a decisive shift.

Iranians cross into Armenia to earn what they cannot at home. Economic crisis is driving some Iranians across the border to Armenia for construction, taxi and delivery work, turning a longtime holiday destination into a source of income for families struggling to make ends meet at home.

Bénin : Romuald Wadagni attendu à Paris pour sa première visite officielle en France. Le président béninois sera à Paris les 4 et 5 octobre pour sa première « visite de travail » depuis son investiture à la tête du pays. Il doit notamment rencontrer son homologue, Emmanuel Macron.

Nucleon Security, la pépite qui défie les géants mondiaux de la cybersécurité. L’éditeur de solutions de cybersécurité veut intensifier son développement sur les marchés d’Afrique subsaharienne, certain de pouvoir se différencier des géants du secteur grâce à sa technologie et son adaptation au terrain.

Avec l’acquisition de Société générale Ghana, Attijariwafa Bank relance son expansion internationale, à pas comptés. Le rachat de Société générale Ghana marque une première incursion stratégique pour le groupe marocain en zone anglophone. Mais l’opération reste modeste et pourrait être confrontée aux aléas monétaires.

En Guinée équatoriale, une nouvelle vague d’expulsions relance le débat sur la libre circulation au sein de la Cemac. Les autorités équato-guinéennes multiplient les arrestations et expulsions d’étrangers originaires d’Afrique centrale. Au cœur des procédures : un différend sur l’application d’un accord signé dans le cadre de la Cemac.

Bras de fer chez Castel : la justice de Singapour relance la lutte pour le contrôle du géant de la bière. Alors que le groupe Castel est l’objet d’un conflit entre la fille du fondateur, Romy Castel, et l’actuel directeur général, Gregory Clerc, une décision de justice à Singapour relance les hostilités. Et pose autant de questions qu’elle donne de réponse.

« Tous les militaires avaient déjà pris le large » : en RDC, la justice militaire se penche sur la chute de Bukavu. Deux généraux, jugés depuis le 25 septembre, sont accusés d’avoir abandonné la capitale du Sud-Kivu en février 2025, pendant l’offensive des rebelles de l’AFC/M23. Des pièces du dossier, obtenues par Jeune Afrique, lèvent le voile sur les dysfonctionnements de l’armée congolaise.

États-Unis – Afrique : comment Donald Trump tente de combler le vide dans les ambassades américaines. Le Congrès américain a validé la nomination de sept nouveaux ambassadeurs en Afrique. Une goutte d’eau, alors que plus de la moitié des postes diplomatiques restent vacants sur le continent après la purge opérée par Trump au début de son mandat. Cartographie.

La première femme nommée à la tête du gouvernement au Maroc, les juntes sahéliennes à l’ONU, l’après-Orano au Niger… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur la nomination de Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri, première femme à la tête du gouvernement marocain, décrypte l’entourage de Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, analyse la stratégie diplomatique commune des juntes sahéliennes, examine la relance de l’uranium au Niger et s’intéresse au pari des solutions solaires pour électrifier l’Afrique rurale.

Avant Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri, une longue lignée de militantes marocaines. S’il répond à une logique institutionnelle, le choix d’une femme, Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri, pour diriger le gouvernement issu des élections du 23 septembre reste un événement. Pourtant, d’autres avant elle ont déjà joué un rôle de premier plan dans l’histoire du royaume.

Afrique de l’Ouest : les véritables ressorts d’une inflation alimentaire tenace. Carburants, engrais, change et météo : les coûts de la chaîne alimentaire s’envolent à nouveau en Afrique de l’Ouest. Une crise structurelle, qui met en lumière les fragilités d’économies encore trop dépendantes des marchés mondiaux. Décryptage en infographies.

Gabon : ces femmes qui font l’économie. Secteur pétrolier, distribution, conseil… Au Gabon, de plus en plus de femmes sont aux commandes dans des secteurs économiques cruciaux. Jeune Afrique a choisi cinq trajectoires qui illustrent cette transformation en cours.

Maroc : ceux (et celles) qui murmurent à l’oreille de Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri. Pour comprendre l’ascension de la nouvelle cheffe du gouvernement, il faut regarder ceux qui l’entourent. Intimes, stratèges, équilibristes ou protégés, ils racontent aussi la trajectoire singulière du Parti Authenticité et Modernité (PAM) et les réseaux sur lesquels la femme politique pourra s’appuyer.

RDC : comment Félix Tshisekedi a externalisé la guerre contre le M23. Face aux combattants du M23 dans l’est de la RDC, la campagne de défense congolaise s’appuie sur des experts extérieurs. Une enquête menée par l’organisation GI-TOC dévoile la manière dont ces prestataires et conseillers opèrent sur le terrain.

Sénégal : décès de l’écrivain et homme d’État Cheikh Hamidou Kane. L’auteur de « L’Aventure ambiguë », classique de la littérature africaine, est décédé dans la soirée du 3 octobre à Dakar à l’âge de 98 ans, ont annoncé la presse et le président sénégalais Bassirou Diomaye Faye.

Cameroun : au RDPC, le silence de Paul Biya suscite le malaise. Un an après une présidentielle contestée et alors que des élections locales sont censées se tenir au début de 2027, le parti au pouvoir au Cameroun est dans l’incertitude, déboussolé par le mutisme de son président national.

Gaz et pétrole : les secrets de la stratégie d’expansion de QatarEnergy en Afrique. Fragilisé par des contraintes opérationnelles majeures consécutives au conflit au Moyen-Orient, le géant du Golfe se cherche de nouveaux relais de croissance et s’appuie sur des projets africains à « fort impact ».

Algérie : la valse des généraux se poursuit à la tête des renseignements militaires. Le général Noureddine Maâche prend la tête de la sécurité de l’armée, sixième patron nommé depuis 2019. Plongée au cœur d’un jeu de chaises musicales généralisé, alimenté par des dissensions avec la présidence.

Gabon : entre Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema et Sylvia Bongo Ondimba, la bataille des récits. Entre le chef de l’État gabonais et les Bongo, la confrontation se poursuit à distance. Depuis plusieurs mois, l’ex-première dame ne cesse de riposter aux accusations de Libreville. De son côté, le nouveau pouvoir entend solder l’héritage de l’ancienne famille présidentielle.

Défense : Israël débarque en force au Marrakech Air Show. Huit entreprises israéliennes, dont trois fournissent déjà les Forces armées royales, participent pour la première fois au Marrakech Air Show, organisé du 7 au 10 octobre. Une présence inédite qui confirme la place prise par l’État hébreu dans la stratégie de défense du royaume, mais aussi ses ambitions en Afrique.

RDC : mort de Kalev Mutond, l’ancien maître-espion qui inspirait le respect et la crainte. Administrateur général de l’Agence nationale de renseignements sous Joseph Kabila, il est décédé à l’âge de 69 ans et laisse le souvenir d’un homme loyal et brutal.

De Casablanca à Abidjan, comment les deux places boursières séduisent les investisseurs étrangers. Les deux places boursières attirent de plus en plus de capitaux venus de l’extérieur. Parmi leurs avantages comparatifs, la stabilité monétaire, des secteurs porteurs et des liquidités en hausse. Explications.

Au Gabon, Prix Import et Carrefour bousculent le géant Ceca-Gadis. Fort du soutien de Carrefour, dont il développe les enseignes en franchise depuis 2021, le groupe local dirigé par Bernard Azzi veut profiter du peu de forme du leader historique du secteur, Ceca-Gadis, pour pousser son avantage.

Déguerpissements en Côte d’Ivoire : pour Alassane Ouattara, l’épineux cas Ibrahim Cissé Bacongo. Après de multiples polémiques, ce fidèle d’Alassane Ouattara, ministre-gouverneur du district d’Abidjan et responsable du parti présidentiel, est au cœur d’un nouveau scandale. Une affaire de nature à susciter le malaise jusqu’au plus haut sommet de l’État.

Reportage à Khartoum : une capitale en ruines, et des rêves de paix lointains. Sous le contrôle de l’armée d’Abdel Fattah al-Burhane depuis dix-huit mois, la métropole soudanaise et ses 7 millions d’habitants tentent peu à peu de reprendre vie. Au milieu des ruines, un comité civil tente d’y organiser un dialogue national, mais l’initiative se heurte au scepticisme de la rue et au rejet de Hemetti.

Levée du moratoire sur la peine de mort : l’opposition algérienne dénonce une « régression ». Après l’Assemblée, c’est au tour du Sénat algérien de débattre de la levée du moratoire sur la peine de mort, qui, a annoncé cet été le président Tebboune, s’appliquerait aux incendiaires et aux ravisseurs d’enfants. L’opposition dénonce l’inefficacité de ce châtiment et le risque d’erreurs judiciaires.

Sénégal : pourquoi Dakar ne sort pas de la crise du logement. Le marché locatif haut de gamme se grippe dans la capitale sénégalaise, où les montants des loyers ont chuté de 10 % à 30 % en deux ans. À l’inverse, la demande reste forte sur les petites surfaces « abordables », pour lesquelles il y a pénurie. État des lieux d’un marché sous tension.

Cameroun : Clément Atangana, le juge qui proclamait les réélections de Paul Biya. Décédé le 4 octobre à Paris, le premier président du Conseil constitutionnel restera dans la mémoire des Camerounais comme le dernier maillon de la chaîne électorale qui reconduisait le président Paul Biya au palais présidentiel d’Etoudi.

5 questions pour comprendre les enjeux de l’agence de notation africaine. Lancée le 7 octobre à Maurice sous le patronage de l’UA, l’Afcra entend offrir une alternative souveraine à la notation financière. Un projet ambitieux qui se heurte au défi majeur de son indépendance.

Togo : comment Faure Gnassingbé a repris la main sur ses bastions électoraux du Nord. Autrefois implantée dans le septentrion togolais, l’opposition y bat désormais de l’aile. Entre intimidations, dissensions et débauchages, analyse des ressorts d’une perte d’influence au profit du parti au pouvoir.

Pourquoi la Banque mondiale alerte sur une nouvelle poussée d’inflation en Afrique subsaharienne. L’intensification des tensions géopolitiques à travers le monde explique la hausse prochaine des prix qui devrait grimper à 5,5 % en 2026, contre 3,7 % en 2025.

Comment l’administration Trump mène son offensive diplomatique contre le droit à l’avortement. Depuis le démantèlement brutal de l’Usaid, des accords bilatéraux, répondant aux intérêts américains, ont remplacé l’aide humanitaire. Le refus de subventionner la promotion ou la pratique de l’avortement en est l’une des dispositions, notamment en Afrique.

Des millions de contraceptifs destinés à des pays africains sont bloqués depuis plus d’un an en Belgique sur décision de l’administration Trump. Financés par l’Usaid, l’agence de développement de Washington, des millions de contraceptifs destinés en grande partie à des pays d’Afrique subsaharienne sont toujours bloqués dans des entrepôts en Belgique.

Dafroza Gauthier, après trente ans de traque des génocidaires rwandais réfugiés en France, est morte. Grâce au Collectif des parties civiles pour le Rwanda (CPCR) que cette ingénieure avait fondé avec son époux Alain Gauthier, sept hommes impliqués dans le génocide des Tutsi en 1994 ont été définitivement condamnés par un tribunal français.

En Egypte, des journalistes mobilisés pour réclamer la libération de six confrères. « Le danger ne se limite pas à ces journalistes. Il concerne tous les journalistes indépendants », a déclaré à l’Agence France-Presse le journaliste Mostafa Bassiouny, présent au rassemblement.

Dans les coulisses de Viginum, la cellule gouvernementale d’experts qui traque les ingérences étrangères sur Internet. Au sein d’une cellule d’experts, ce service traque les évolutions du cyberespace, sur TikTok ou ailleurs. Les « attaquants » sont parfois étatiques, parfois non, ce qui nécessite d’avoir une approche globale, sur tout un écosystème.

Paul-Simon Handy, chercheur : « L’Afrique a réussi à corriger le planisphère, elle doit maintenant pouvoir rectifier sa propre place au sein du système mondial ». Les résolutions de l’ONU sur la traite transatlantique et sur la représentation cartographique du monde ont remis au premier plan les questions de réparation et de la position du continent africain dans l’ordre international. Reste à transformer ces succès en gains politiques et économiques, estime le spécialiste dans un entretien au « Monde ».

Cheikh Hamidou Kane, écrivain sénégalais et figure de la littérature africaine, est mort à l’âge de 98 ans. Figure de la littérature africaine et ancien ministre, Cheikh Hamidou Kane laisse derrière lui une œuvre qui a marqué l’enseignement et la réflexion sur l’identité à travers le continent.

Howard W. French, écrivain : « L’Afrique doit trouver ses propres moyens d’élaborer des projets nationaux et continentaux, la solution ne viendra pas d’ailleurs ». Le journaliste et auteur consacre son dernier ouvrage à Kwame Nkrumah, héraut du panafricanisme et père de l’indépendance du Ghana, en 1957. Horward W. French explique, dans un entretien au « Monde », que la montée en puissance de l’Afrique sur la scène internationale dépend notamment de l’union de ses Etats.

Ebola en RDC : Jean-Noël Barrot témoigne du soutien de Paris à Kinshasa. Jean-Noël Barrot s’est rendu en République démocratique du Congo, dans la province d’Ituri, pour marquer le soutien de la France face à l’épidémie du virus Ebola la plus meurtrière de l’histoire du pays.

En Ethiopie, la prise de Makalé par l’armée fédérale ravive les craintes d’un conflit régional dans la Corne de l’Afrique. Après des mois de tensions, les combats ont repris fin septembre dans le nord de l’Ethiopie, entre d’une part l’armée fédérale et, d’autre part, le Front populaire de libération du Tigré.

Au Nigeria, un avion de l’armée de l’air s’écrase dans le sud du pays avec 32 personnes à bord. L’appareil, qui assurait un vol de routine entre Benin City et Lagos, est tombé près d’une base navale de l’Etat d’Ondo, où des recherches ont été lancées. Le président nigérian a confirmé qu’il n’y avait aucun survivant.

En Ethiopie, l’armée fédérale met en échec l’offensive rebelle, la région craint l’embrasement. Après la reprise, samedi 3 octobre, de Makalé, la capitale régionale du Tigré, par l’armée fédérale, une éventuelle intervention de l’Erythrée, alliée des rebelles, concentre désormais toutes les inquiétudes.

En Ethiopie, Abiy Ahmed reconduit à la tête du gouvernement, en pleine guerre au Tigré. Some disappeared during Israeli ground attacks on their neighbourhoods or displacement camps. Others went missing while searching for aid, checking on their homes or travelling near the so-called Yellow Line . For their families, the absence of any definitive answer has left them suspended between hope and grief, unsure whether to keep waiting or begin mourning. According to the Independent Commission for Human Rights , more than 11,000 people in Gaza remain unaccounted for, including those believed to be buried beneath the rubble and those suspected of enforced disappearance. The Palestinian Centre for Missing and Forcibly Disappeared estimates that between 2,500 and 3,000 people are suspected of enforced disappearance, having gone missing or lost contact with their families since the start of the war and through the ceasefire announced on 9 October 2025. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Their fate remains unknown, with Israeli authorities still withholding the names of all those detained from the Strip and failing to identify approximately 620 bodies returned to Gaza. For the families left behind, the disappearance of a loved one has become a daily ordeal. They live with the agonising uncertainty of not knowing whether their relatives are alive, detained, buried beneath the rubble or among the unidentified dead. Middle East Eye spoke to three families whose relatives disappeared during the war about their hopes, fears and the long wait for answers. Nidal al-Waheedi, 32 (at the time of disappearance) “If I knew he had been killed, I would have accepted it like everyone else. But we do not even know whether he is alive or dead.” Nidal al-Waheedi's father hold a picture of him before his disappearance on 7 October 2023 (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Inside a small tent on al-Nafaq Street in central Gaza City, Nidal al-Waheedi’s parents scroll through photographs of their son on a mobile phone. The pictures are among the few things they have left of him after their home was bombed and his belongings destroyed. “We have nothing to do but look at his pictures and wait,” his father, Suhail al-Waheedi, 62, told Middle East Eye. 'He was the backbone of our family' - Suhail al-Waheedi, Palestinian father “For three years, all we have done is wait and hope for any news about our son.” Nidal, a journalist, disappeared in the early hours of 7 October 2023. He had left with colleagues to cover events at the Erez crossing in northern Gaza following the Hamas attack on the Israeli checkpoint. Minutes after arriving at the site, his family lost contact with him. “Nidal is never far from our thoughts. We try to stay hopeful and keep waiting for some word from him,” his father said. But the family has also grown increasingly frustrated with rights organisations. Al-Waheedi said he contacted the Red Cross and other organisations, but received no information about his son. “None of the appeals we made to rights organisations helped us. In this war, sadly, there is no respect for human rights. Nidal al-Waheedi's parents say they have nothing left of him except for a few photos on their phones (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); For al-Waheedi, what hurts most is not only not knowing what happened to his son, but living without the person he once relied on every day. “Nidal was not just our son. He was our friend, the backbone of our family and my righthand man. I miss him most now. I keep thinking about how much easier these difficult days would be if he were here.” Saeed Hajjaj, 59, and Qasem Hajjaj, 17 (at the time of disappearance) “The pain of losing my father and brother has left us in a constant state of grief. We do not attend weddings, and we have not eaten sweets for more than two years.” Nisreen Hajjaj holds photos of Qasem Hajjaj (L) and Saeed Hajjaj (R), who have been missing since Israeli troops seized them on 26 December 2023 (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE) Before going to sleep, Mona Hajjaj, 52, sits on her mattress inside the tent where she is displaced at Palestine Stadium in central Gaza City. After taking her heart medication, she and her two daughters talk about memories of her husband, Saeed, and son, Qasem. The family lost contact with both men on 26 December 2023. “My mother developed heart problems from the grief of losing my father and younger brother,” Nisreen Hajjaj, 35, told MEE. “Her eyesight also became weaker because she cried day and night, missing them and not knowing what had happened to them.” The family had been staying with relatives in Sheikh Radwan, northern Gaza City, when they became trapped on 20 December during the Israeli invasion. After raiding the area and destroying surrounding homes, Israeli forces stormed Hajjaj’s house. The women were forced to leave for southern Gaza, while the men were detained. “The last time we saw my father and brother was when they were naked, handcuffed, tortured and humiliated. Since then, we have known nothing about them - where they are or what condition they are in,” Nisreen said. The family has contacted rights organisations seeking information, but received no answers. 'They are still part of our lives, but we do not know whether to mourn them or wait for them' - Nisreen Hajjaj, Gaza resident The uncertainty has seeped into every part of their lives. “They are still part of our lives, but we do not know whether to mourn them or wait for them,” Nisreen said. “We have been left without the people we depended on. Sadly, support organisations do not deal with us because they are not listed as martyrs or prisoners.” Hajjaj refuses to accept that they may have died in the incident without official confirmation. Even after all these years, she still hopes to hear news about them. “My sister was offered a scholarship to cover her university expenses, but we had to provide a death certificate. We refused and gave up the scholarship because we do not want to accept that fate while there is still a glimmer of hope that he may come home alive.” The Hajjaj family’s loss has affected more than their finances and daily lives; it has also taken away the family moments they had hoped to share. “My brother’s wife was nine months pregnant, and my father was eagerly waiting to meet his first grandchild,” said Nisreen. “Becoming a grandfather was his dream. Now, Alaa waits for released detainees, showing them his brother’s photograph and asking whether they saw him or heard his name. “Many nights, I fall asleep in tears because I miss my brother and the support he gave me. It also breaks my heart that his eldest son was killed and we could not protect him while his father was gone,” he said. Since neighbouring Eritrea gained independence in 1993, Ethiopia has been landlocked, as the newly created state took away the port of Assab and with it Ethiopia's access to the sea. Earlier this year, a former Ethiopian government adviser told Middle East Eye that Ethiopia's key ally, the United Arab Emirates , was "calling the shots" in regard to Eritrea and any Ethiopian plans to retake Assab by force. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Since 1993, Ethiopia has relied on the port of Djibouti for sea access, but it has long sought alternative arrangements. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland, the breakaway region of Somalia also backed by the UAE and recognised by Israel , that envisaged access to the sea and a potential naval presence. Inside Somaliland: How Berbera Port is central to the Red Sea's power struggle Read More » Somalia condemned the agreement as a violation of its sovereignty, although relations between Addis Ababa and Mogadishu subsequently improved. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud said the country did not object to Ethiopia gaining access to the sea through Somali territory. “I look forward to working closely together to strengthen Somalia-Ethiopia relations & advance peace, stability & shared prosperity for our peoples & the Horn of Africa,” Mohamud said in a post congratulating Abiy on his new term. Ethiopia's other neighbours have taken a harder line. On Sunday, the leaders of Egypt , Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia met in Egypt's New Alamein and issued a joint declaration affirming “the principle of freedom of navigation”, while saying that “the governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of the littoral states”. The declaration also called for respect for international law governing transboundary rivers, including the Nile, and rejected unilateral measures affecting the existing water uses of Egypt and Sudan. In April, MEE revealed that an Ethiopian army base was being used to support the UAE-backed Rapid Support Forces in the Sudan war. Dispute over maritime access Ethiopia’s push for Red Sea access has become a growing source of tension with its neighbours. While Addis Ababa sees this as necessary to ensure the country’s economic and geopolitical security, Eritrea, Egypt, Sudan, and Somalia have stressed that coastal states have jurisdiction over their territorial waters. Exclusive: The Ethiopian army base covertly supporting Sudan’s RSF Read More » Somalia has opened the possibility of granting Ethiopia conditional access to the sea, if the two countries reach a formal agreement. The dispute comes as fighting has intensified in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, with government-aligned forces retaking the regional capital Mekele after renewed clashes with Tigrayan forces. The escalation has raised fears of the conflict spiralling into a larger regional confrontation. Eritrea finds itself in the middle of the discord, as Ethiopia has long sought to gain access to the Red Sea through Eritrean ports. The two neighbouring states have had a hostile relationship for decades, with Eritrea cutting diplomatic ties with Ethiopia last week after Addis Ababa closed its embassy in Asmara and expelled ten Eritrean diplomats. This deterioration in relations comes on the heels of the two countries’ dispute with Egypt and Sudan over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, which threatens to divert water from the Nile. The African Union has called for restraint and dialogue as hostilities in northern Ethiopia intensify, urging the parties to seek a peaceful resolution to the crisis. For this reason, "Israel Proper" is incapable of substantial de-occupation. It is capable of token gestures. The only time Israel withdrew settlers from Gaza in 2005, under the premiership of Ariel Sharon, it made sure that the total number of settlers that year was increased, by allowing more settlers into the West Bank than had been withdrawn from Gaza. But it banks its territorial gains as it does the concessions that one generation of Palestinian leaders after another gives them. And here lies Miliband’s problem or, to be specific, the problem of sanctioning Israel to save the two-state solution, or to save Israel from itself. Put aside the fact that there are no negotiations or any likelihood of them for years to come. Put aside, too, the fact that the Palestinian leaders capable of uniting all factions are either in prison or have been assassinated. The West wants Netanyahu gone - so Palestinians can be killed more quietly again Read More » Just ask yourself one practical question: which Israeli leader, born or yet to be born, is capable of forcing over one million Jewish settlers from their homes, businesses, farms and industrial estates in the West Bank and East Jerusalem? The two-state solution could have happened once. But that train left the station almost a quarter of a century ago when Israel rejected the Arab Peace Initiative. There is not a single member of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office who believes that Israel, under any leadership, would allow a Palestinian state to be born. The motions in the Knesset banning a Palestinian state, with overwhelming majorities, tell the same story. So Miliband’s two-state solution is as much a mirage as the progressive Zionist attempts to argue for the existence of an "Israel Proper". Neither exist nor are likely to. The shrinking of Palestine Instead, what exists day by day, one ripped up olive tree at a time, is the steady erosion and shrinking of Palestine in any form. This campaign involves every arm of the Israeli state. The army is a citizen’s army and has the full support of its Jewish citizens, of every political colour. Global inaction is consent. Israel is intensely aware of global opinion, and as one window of rapid expansion is about to close, it makes hay while the sun shines. The rate of expansion in 2025 reached its highest level in 20 years. This conflict will end only when Arabs and Jews live together as equal citizens in the same space There are brave Israelis who put their bodies between the Palestinians and the sticks and guns of the settlers. There are braver Israelis who document all the human rights abuses. But their numbers can be counted on the fingers of several hands. Supporters of two states argue that one state is a recipe for permanent conflict. But a state of war exists at the moment. The only thing that fluctuates is its intensity. This conflict will end only when Arabs and Jews live together as equal citizens in the same space. There are many creative solutions as to what you call that space, and whether it will be one or two states or a confederation of them. Whatever you call it, its citizens have to share basic things like equality before justice, equal shares of housing, land, water, security, airspace, irrespective of ethnicity or religion. The Green Party motion may be intensely uncomfortable for the older generation of practising Jew in Britain. It may indeed challenge their identity as Jews or as liberals. It may disturb their vision of Israel. But that shock may yet prove to be salutary. As they pray peacefully and safely in Britain’s synagogues, practising Jews can at least be comforted by the fact that they will not be shot at, spat at, bludgeoned or teargassed by paramilitary police, and their place of worship regularly stormed by religious fascist mobs. This is the weekly experience of Muslims who attempt to pray at Al Aqsa Mosque or indeed of Christian worshippers as they pray at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. This, too, is a product of "Israel Proper", a Jewish supremacist state that regards all non-Jews as potential or real threats. Allow this state of affairs to continue and there will not be a Palestine left to campaign for. Which is precisely what Israel and its backers are gunning for. ICC confirms Middle East Eye reporting on Afghanistan arrest warrants Submitted by Sondos Asem on Tue, 10/06/2026 - 13:01 Judges unseal court documents showing arrest warrants issued last year for senior Taliban figures for gender persecution Afghan women walk along a street in the Dand district of Afghanistan's Kandahar province on 5 October 2026 (Sanaullah SEIAM/AFP) Off The International Criminal Court (ICC) decided on Monday to make public two additional arrest warrants for members of the Taliban that were issued secretly last year. As previously revealed by Middle East Eye, the two warrants were issued confidentially by a panel of three judges in September 2025 and came two months after public warrants were issued for two leaders of the group, which now forms the government of Afghanistan. The four are facing charges of the crime against humanity of persecution on gender and political grounds, allegedly committed by the Taliban as the de facto government authority in Afghanistan from at least 15 August 2021 until at least 20 January 2025. In July 2025, the ICC issued public arrest warrants for the Taliban's supreme leader Hibatullah Akhundzada and Abdul Hakim Haqqani, Afghanistan’s chief justice. The court has now named the two other suspects as Afghanistan’s minister of education, Habibullah Agha , and acting minister of higher education Neda Mohammad Nadim . (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The ICC said on Monday that the four Taliban members are accused of criminal responsibility for ordering or soliciting the crime against humanity of persecution on gender grounds against girls, women and other persons non-conforming with the group’s policy on gender, gender identity or expression. It added that they are also accused of persecution on political grounds against persons perceived as “allies of girls and women”. “While the Taliban have imposed certain rules and prohibitions on the population as a whole, they have specifically targeted girls and women by reason of their gender, depriving them of fundamental rights and freedoms,” the court said. Exclusive: ICC issued two secret arrest warrants for Taliban members for gender persecution Read More » “Specifically, the Taliban severely deprived, through decrees and edicts, girls and women of the rights to education, privacy and family life and the freedoms of movement, expression, thought, conscience and religion,” it added. “In addition, other persons were targeted because certain expressions of sexuality and/or gender identity were regarded as inconsistent with the Taliban’s policy on gender.” The four warrants set a historic precedent under international law. They mark the first time the ICC or any other international tribunal has recognised LGBTQ+ victims. The charge of gender persecution is also very rare under international law, and there has never been a conviction on it. The charge has been prosecuted just once by the ICC, in the Al Hassan case , but never led to a conviction. The four applications were prepared under the leadership of former prosecutor Karim Khan and Nazhat Shameem Khan, the ICC's deputy prosecutor, who oversees the Afghanistan investigation. The team has been guided by Lisa Davis, a special adviser who authored the office’s policy on gender persecution. In April last year, judges ordered the prosecutor’s office not to publicise any requests for arrest warrants unless authorised by a chamber. But according to the court’s amended regulations , chambers may decide on a case-to-case basis to make warrants public to stop or deter the commission of criminal acts or to improve chances of arrest. US pressure on ICC Meanwhile, as also previously reported by MEE, the court has made public a request by the judges for the office of the prosecutor to open a standalone investigation into allegations of gender persecution by the Taliban, separating it from the court's long-running Afghanistan war crimes probe that covered US nationals. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); If prosecutors proceed, the Taliban investigation will effectively be split from a broader Afghanistan inquiry looking into alleged war crimes committed since 2003 by Afghan National Security Forces, the US military and CIA personnel, in addition to the Taliban and the Islamic State-Khorasan Province (IS-K) group. Exclusive: ICC judges order Taliban case split from Afghanistan probe that covers US troops Read More » The move is likely to raise questions about whether the court is seeking to ease tensions with Washington by signalling that it will no longer pursue allegations against US forces and their allies. The chamber's communication came days after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio threatened to “dismantle the ICC, brick by brick”, in remarks referencing the court's 2020 decision authorising an investigation into alleged crimes committed in Afghanistan. Since February 2025, the US has imposed retaliatory financial and visa sanctions on court officials in connection with the Afghanistan and Palestine investigations, citing efforts to prosecute nationals or allies of the US. ​​The first target was Karim Khan , the former prosecutor of the ICC, who was controversially removed by member states in July after an 18-month-long misconduct probe. Also targeted were nine judges, three of whom - Kimberly Prost, Solomy Bossa and Luz Ibanez - were members of the 2020 Appeals Chamber that authorised the Afghanistan investigation. The sanctions came despite the decision by Khan in 2021 to deprioritise the strand of the Afghanistan probe concerning US military and CIA personnel, as well as former Afghan government forces, in order to focus the investigation on the Taliban and the Islamic State-Khorasan Province. MEE reported in December that diplomats at the ICC's annual Assembly of States Parties meeting in The Hague said the Trump administration had pressed the court to drop its investigations into Afghanistan and Palestine as a condition for lifting sanctions. It also demanded that states amend the ICC’s founding treaty - the Rome Statute - to prevent the prosecution of nationals from countries that aren’t members of the court, such as the US and Israel . At the end of its meeting, however, the assembly issued a declaration resisting those demands and rejecting calls to amend the Rome Statute, without naming the US directly. The TV network swiftly cancelled the contract after Mediapart told France Televisions it would publish its findings about the deal. According to Mediapart, the broadcaster’s management pushed through the appointment of Terrific to collect audience data for France 2’s flagship political programme “L’Heure de Vérité” (The Moment of Truth). France Televisions is France’s most-watched television group, with its channels together accounting for 29.4 percent of TV viewing in 2025, according to its annual results . Employees feared that giving the Israeli company access to sensitive data ahead of the 2027 presidential and legislative elections would threaten France’s security. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Founded in 2021, Terrific describes itself as a marketing and audience measurement agency. Its website lists partnerships with major technology companies, including Google, TikTok, Meta and LinkedIn. Terrific’s founder, Israel Grintz, also heads NEAIG, a start-up specialising in political marketing, according to the Israeli newspaper Haaretz . Its other shareholder is Natan Eshel. 'Each time, the response was the same: ''Management wants to see this project through, we have to go ahead, it comes from higher up''' - Mediapart Eshel served as Netanyahu’s chief of staff between 2010 and 2012 and has remained a close adviser to the Israeli prime minister and his wife, Sara. “From the moment the project was awarded to Terrific until the decision to definitively pull the plug, France Televisions management was fully aware of the risks involved,” said Mediapart. “Numerous warnings were issued to several of the company's executives very early on. Each time, the response was the same: 'Management wants to see this project through, we have to go ahead, it comes from higher up',” the outlet reported. France Televisions intended to use Terrific’s tool throughout the presidential campaign. Mediapart reported that its methods of aggregating data raised fears of foreign interference. The company combines data from tracking tools embedded in applications it designs with clients. Such data could identify users’ political leanings and allow advertisers to target them with messages tailored to their views. Employees feared that a foreign state could weaponise the tool to deliver personalised political advertising. Israeli interference in French elections 'Attack on our democracy': Inside an Israeli influence campaign in France's local elections Read More » Evidence of Israeli interference in French elections has already emerged. Earlier this year, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nunez, said authorities would take legal action after revelations that an Israeli firm called BlackCore had run a disinformation campaign against left-leaning candidates during municipal elections in March. Anne-Sophie Dhiver, deputy head of Viginum, France’s agency for combating online disinformation, told parliament that “a private company based in Israel that specialises in selling online destabilisation services” had attacked candidates who opposed Israel’s genocide in Gaza and apartheid in the occupied West Bank . Dhiver said the agency could not identify who sponsored the campaign. The Israeli government has also drawn closer in recent years to National Rally, France’s main far-right party, which leads opinion polls. } } catch (e) {} } })(); The government on Monday increased the price of petrol by Re0.88 per litre, but reduced that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs1.88 per litre. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs393.64 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs397.76 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 6 (Tuesday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Pakistan, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia agree to rapid force deployment in the kingdom under Makkah pact. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye have agreed to deploy military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Monday following an emergency meeting of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Riyadh. The three countries held an emergency meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) of the Makkah Defence Alliance to address the security developments and threats facing Saudi Arabia, the FO statement said. “The committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the parties, thereby enhancing readiness, military integration, and the collective capacity to confront and counter threats,” it added. While the statement did not specifically name any threat, the development comes against the backdrop of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in the Yemen conflict. In the Riyadh meeting, the three members of the Makkah Defence Alliance condemned “in the strongest terms” the attempted targeting of Makkah and Madina, as well as the continuing attacks targeting cities and civilian and economic facilities in Saudi Arabia, reaffirming their “unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the kingdom’s security and territorial integrity”, the statement said. For their part, Pakistan and Turkiye commended the “vigilance and readiness of the Saudi armed forces, as well as the professionalism and high level of competence they have demonstrated in countering the threats and attacks facing the kingdom and in safeguarding its security and territorial integrity”, the FO said. The SPDC reviewed the outcomes of the political and military consultations preceding the meeting and approved the recommendations submitted to it, affirming that the Makkah pact embodied a firm commitment to collective defence and a unified position in confronting threats, it said. Moreover, the three countries affirmed that the security of each member of the alliance was an “integral part of the collective security of the three countries, and that translating the Makkah Agreement for Joint Defence into practical measures demonstrates the credibility of the commitment to collective defence, strengthens the effectiveness of deterrence, and reaffirms the unity and determination of our three countries to defend their security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, in accordance with the provisions of the agreement”. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, joined Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ via telephone and said Saudi Arabia had made “gains and recovered some areas” in Yemen in the ongoing fighting with the Houthis. When asked about a possible operational role by Pakistan and Turkiye, the defence minister replied that both nations had a “presence in theatre”, but only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. “Whatever assistance they require is being provided. But right now, the Turkish and Pakistani armies are playing a supportive role,” he said, noting that Pakistan was involved in reconnaissance. The defence minister said the meeting was primarily focused on formalising the Makkah alliance’s operational structure. “The organisational structure of the alliance was formalised during today’s meeting,” he said. As part of the institutional development of the Makkah alliance, the SPDC decided to appoint Pakistan’s Lieutenant General (Retd) Nauman Mahmood as the first secretary general of the alliance for a three-year term, the FO statement said. “The parties welcomed him, wished him every success in the discharge of his duties, and expressed their confidence in his contribution to advancing the alliance and achieving its objectives,” it added. In an earlier statement on social media platform X, the FO said Pakistan’s delegation to the meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) included Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and Asif. “The meeting will also be attended by the respective ministers of foreign affairs, ministers of defence, as well as chiefs of general staff of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and the Republic of Türkiye,” the FO added. The Makkah defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. The SPDC meeting under it has been held as Yemen’s Saudi-led coalition government launched a major military campaign on Sunday to recapture territory held by the Houthis. Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis showed no signs of abating over the weekend, with the Houthis saying the kingdom had launched dozens of strikes on Yemen’s capital Sanaa, after which they attacked an Aramco facility with ballistic missiles and drones south of Riyadh. The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait in a lightning offensive. On Sept 25, the military chiefs of Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia met in Riyadh for urgently convened talks under the pact in light of the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Sept 18, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry had expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, saying Pakistan will go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”. Defence Minister Asif also earlier reaffirmed that Pakistan would “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalated.

Phishing domains impersonate govt agencies. ISLAMABAD: The National Cyber Security Emergency Response Team (NCERT) has detected a number of suspected phishing domains created in the name of key national institutions, apparently aimed at stealing sensitive information from citizens. According to the NCERT’s Threat Intelligence Centre, suspicious domains impersonating several government and public sector organisations were found active on Sunday (Oct 4). The identified domains include a suspected “secure login” domain impersonating the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra), while phishing domains using names like the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), the Higher Education Commission (HEC), the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) and the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) were also detected. Likewise, suspicious domains impersonating the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP), the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) and the Prime Minister’s Youth Programme were identified. NCERT advises public not to share personal information on unauthorised websites The Threat Intelligence Centre also spotted a suspicious login domain using the name of Punjab Safe Cities. The NCERT said the suspected phishing domains were still active and their activities were being monitored. It warned that phishing websites and impersonation-based attacks could be used to deceive users into entering sensitive information, including login credentials and other personal data. The NCERT advised citizens and government organisations to exercise caution while accessing links, websites and login pages received through unverified sources. It urged users to verify the authenticity of websites before entering personal information and said monitoring of phishing activities and impersonation of national institutions was in progress. Safe use of GenAI At the same time, National Cert has issued an advisory for “safe and secure use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools and platforms”. The rapid adoption of public AI chatbots, coding assistants, browser extensions, AI-enabled applications, and third-party AI services is creating new cybersecurity and data governance risks across organisations, the agency observed. It added that uncontrolled or unauthorised use of Generative AI, commonly referred to as Shadow AI, may expose sensitive information, intellectual property, credentials, source code, and organisational data while introducing risks from prompt injection, insecure AI-generated code, malicious integrations, inaccurate outputs, and compromised third-party models. The NCERT has advised organisations to protect “sensitive and classified information, strictly prohibit the submission of classified, confidential, sensitive, personal, proprietary, credential-related, or otherwise restricted organisational information to public or unapproved AI platforms. Organisations have been directed to establish an approved AI tool registry, while maintaining a centrally vetted and regularly reviewed inventory of authorised AI tools, models, browser extensions, plug-ins, APIs, and platforms. The advice added that organisations should remain on the vigil for sensitive data exposure, Shadow AI, unauthorised AI plug-ins, suspicious AI access and policy violations. The cybersecurity agency added that wherever an AI-related incident occurs, organisations should immediately contain unauthorised access. Organisations were also advised to preserve evidence and logs, revoke compromised credentials or API keys, investigate exposure, implement corrective measures and report the incident to the NCERT.
