IMF talks likely to clear way for $1.2bn disbursement. ISLAMABAD: Pakis­tan’s ongoing talks with a visiting staff mission of the International Monet­ary Fund (IMF) are set to conclude on a positive note later this week, paving the way for the disbursement of about $1.2 billion under two concurrent progra­mmes — the $7bn Exten­ded Fund Facility (EFF) and the $1.4bn Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF). Informed sources said the two sides were now finalising the Memor­andum of Econ­omic and Fiscal Policies (MEFP) after covering the substantive parameters of the biannual review. Following the completion of the draft exchanges, the staff mission, led by Ms Iva Petrova, is expected to conclude its visit in the next couple of days, official sources said. There were no new demands from the Fund, except for makeup adjustments to bridge past slippages. The revenue target remains unchanged, with a greater focus on achieving the half-yearly target following robust collection in the first quarter, which exceeded the target. The development comes as the authorities struggle to finalise the liquefied natural gas (LNG) import plan for the upcoming three winter months — December to February — amid a challenging supply situation stemming from the US-Iran conflict. The gas companies and the petroleum division had sought at least 22 import cargoes for the three-month period, but the task force on energy, led by Lt Gen Zafar Iqbal, has promised no more than 10-12 cargoes of around 100 million cubic feet each on a best-effort basis, using all diplomatic and logistical channels. The plan will be presented to the prime minister for approval, given the involvement of around $100m per spot cargo and the requirement for consent from the Ministry of Finance and the State Bank of Pakistan. The matter has assumed greater importance because the LNG import plan will affect the current account targets agreed upon by the Ministry of Finance and the IMF. Sources, however, indicated that actual LNG imports may not exceed seven to eight cargoes over the three winter months, given prevailing market conditions, which would bring the outcome closer to the Ministry of Finance’s desired level. The two sides have agreed to expedite groundwork for targeted subsidies in the gas sector through the social protection programme to contain gas-sector circular debt and move BISP-based subsidies for the poorest consumers in the power sector into the implementation phase, starting January next year following the introduction of the revised base tariff. The distribution companies have already filed tariff petitions during the course of the talks to demonstrate their preparedness to the IMF team, the sources said. The government has assured the Fund of plans to reduce cross-subsidies from the industrial sector and contain gas-sector debt, which has now reached Rs3.6 trillion and continues to rise. This includes principal payables of around Rs1.8 trillion and almost an equivalent amount in accrued interest and late-payment surcharges. The gas companies have reported that the introduction of a protected category for domestic consumers, involving gas prices of Rs200-350 per mmBtu, has aggravated the pricing gap and, consequently, increased circular debt. Only four of the 12 consumer slabs covered the cost of gas supply during the winter months, while the remaining eight remained below breakeven rates for around eight months despite the imposition of substantial fixed charges. Although these measures are not being defined as prior actions, the authorities may have to take a few steps between the conclusion of the ongoing IMF talks and the scheduling of the Fund’s Executive Board meeting to ensure smooth processing of Pakistan’s case for the disbursement of $1.2bn and seek waivers for a couple of unavoidable slippages that had already occurred against the end-June 2026 targets. An IMF structural benchmark committed by the government requires a major policy reform by end-January 2027 to replace the budgeted tariff-differential subsidy and cross-subsidy system with a targeted, budgeted subsidy framework for low-income consumers through BISP. The World Bank is assisting the government in linking power consumers to the National Socio-Economic Registry. The government has undertaken to complete the technical linkage, along with validity checks, by end-November to determine eligibility criteria. The IMF is now also pushing for greater transparency in the Inland Freight Equalisation Margin (IFEM), which facilitates uniform petroleum pricing across the country. Moscow moot ends sans joint statement. • Pakistan-Afghanistan disagreement cited as main reason • Islamabad maintains cross-border terror attacks rose despite peace talks with Taliban • ICC unseals warrants for Afghan ministers over anti-women actions ISLAMABAD: The eighth edition of the Moscow Format regional consultations on Afghanistan on Monday ended without a joint communique, mainly because of disagreements between Pakistani and Afghan delegations in what was possibly the first instance in the series where participants failed to agree on a joint statement. Russian presidential envoy for Afghanistan Zamir Kabulov said Moscow regretted that the participants could not agree on the final document. “When drafting the final joint statement, we encountered one problem, that problem was that our Afghan and Pakistani colleagues didn’t see eye to eye,” he said. The Moscow meeting brought together special envoys and senior officials from Afghanistan, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, with Belarus and Egypt attending as guests. The format dates back to 2016 -17 and has emerged as one of the main regional diplomatic tracks on Afghanistan. The failure to agree on a joint statement underscored how the worsening Pakistan-Afghanistan dispute is now complicating wider regional efforts to build consensus on Afghanistan. The tense relations between Islamabad and Kabul were among the key issues discussed at the meeting, with the dispute over terrorism and counterterrorism language ultimately preventing the adoption of the joint document. Mr Kabulov said the Afghan side objected to references that placed Afghanistan in a terrorist context. Attacks from Afghan soil Pakistan’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Moha­mmad Sadiq, told the meeting that Islamabad wanted peace and stability in the region and had pursued political and diplomatic engagement with the Taliban leadership to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil. “Pakistan desires peace and stability in the region and has remained patiently engaged in political and diplomatic efforts aimed at addressing the menace of terrorism emanating from Afghan soil. However, it is unfortunate that Pakistan’s numerous goodwill gestures and highly responsible appr­oach were misconstrued, resulting in increased terrorist attacks from Afghan soil, with the active support and backing of the Taliban Regime,” he said. Taliban want more talks Afghan Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi, meanwhile, criticised Pakistan’s statements and actions towards Afghanistan and Afghans, accusing Islamabad of using military pressure, refugees, students and transit routes as instruments of leverage. At the same time, he insisted that the problems affecting relations bet­ween the two neighbours could be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy. Russia offered to help de-escalate the dispute, although Kabulov stressed that resolving bilateral disputes was not the purpose of the Moscow Format. “Russia is ready to assist in ending this conflict in any possible, permissible way either on its own or in partnership with our other partners provided that both sides make such a request. We are ready to provide the maximum possible assistance,” he said. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who opened the meeting, endorsed the performance of the Taliban authorities while warning against any attempt by Nato to establish military infrastructure in Afghanistan or neighbouring countries. He backed assistance to Kabul and said strengthening Afghanistan’s counterterrorism capacity served regional interests. ICC warrants Meanwhile, the Inter­national Criminal Court on Monday unsealed arrest warrants for two Afghan ministers accused of committing crimes against humanity through the Taliban government’s restrictions on women and girls, AFP reported. The warrants, for Habibullah Agha, minister of education, and Neda Mohammad Nadeem, minister of higher education, were issued in September 2025 but remained under seal until Monday. The two officials are accused of gender-based persecution linked to policies that have barred girls from attending school beyond primary level and excluded women from higher education following the Taliban’s return to power in August 2021. The two warrants against the ministers were issued after the ICC, in July 2025, authorised warrants for Afghanistan’s Supreme Taliban Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and Supreme Court President Abdul Hakim Haqqani, parts of which have been made public. Both Agha and Nadeem were instrumental in imposing the supreme leader’s vision of Afghanistan. In a sharp reaction to the ICC warrants, a Taliban spokesman condemned the ICC position on the arrest of Afghan leaders. Published in Dawn, October 6th, 2026

Pakistan opposes new permanent Security Council members. • Asim Iftikhar says Islamabad backs more elected seats on UNSC • Foreign secretary-designate highlights country’s role in peaceful dispute settlement • Notes Islamabad presses for peaceful settlement of Kashmir dispute WASHINGTON: Pakistan opposes adding new permanent members to the UN Security Council and instead favours increasing the number of elected, non-permanent members of the 15-member body, Pakistan’s UN envoy Ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad, who is set to take charge as the country’s new foreign secretary next week, told Dawn. Assessing Pakistan’s stint on the Security Council, from 2025 to 2026, he discussed the major international crises and diplomatic initiatives that marked his tenure. Mr Ahmad is returning to Islamabad after serving as Pakistan’s permanent representative to the UN and will take charge as the new foreign secretary. “Developments in recent years in the peace and security landscape and within the Security Council, as well as increased criticism of the role of the permanent members, have further reinforced the belief of a wide majority of member states that we need a more democratic, representative and accountable Security Council,” he said. “Adding any new individual permanent members would only aggravate the problem. In simple words, the problem cannot be the solution.” Pakistan, he said, had advocated, along with members of the Uniting for Consensus group and other like-minded countries, a reformed Council with more elected members, including medium-term seats based on periodic elections and rotation. “Pakistan and many other countries are eminently qualified to bring their contribution to the Security Council and the maintenance of international peace and security,” Mr Ahmad said. “Member states should be ready to fulfil that responsibility without permanence and privilege.” Pakistan’s 2025-26 term was its eighth tenure on the Security Council. For Mr Ahmad personally, it was his third consecutive Council assignment, having previously served on Pakistan’s teams in 2003-04 and 2012-13. “It is such a great and singular honour to have the opportunity to represent Pakistan at the United Nations including at the Security Council,” he said. He said Pakistan entered its latest Council term with considerable diplomatic and institutional experience and had identified conflict prevention and peaceful settlement of disputes, peacekeeping, counterterrorism and cooperation with regional organisations as key priorities. “We were able to achieve a lot in all of those domains,” he said. The term, however, unfolded against a backdrop of deep geopolitical tensions, including a sharp deterioration in relations between India and Pakistan that culminated in a four-day military confrontation in May 2025 , bringing the two nuclear-armed neighbours dangerously close to a wider conflict. Mr Ahmad said the crisis also reinforced Pakistan’s emphasis on peaceful settlement of disputes and highlighted the importance of diplomacy in preventing conflicts from escalating. He pointed to Security Council Resolution 2788, adopted unanimously during Pakistan’s presidency of the Council in July 2025, as one of the major achievements of the country’s term. The Pakistan-sponsored resolution placed renewed emphasis on the mechanisms provided by the UN Charter for the peaceful settlement of international disputes. Despite what Mr Ahmad described as a “polarised Council”, Pakistan was able to forge consensus around the resolution. “This landmark resolution has been the most widely referred Council decision ever since its adoption, something that testifies to its importance and relevance to Council’s work,” he said. “It is also worth recalling that Pakistan initiated and steered this resolution that lays emphasis on peaceful resolution of disputes, having inflicted a crushing defeat to the Indian aggression in May 2025,” he said. Mr Ahmad also highlighted what he described as Pakistan’s practical contribution to peaceful dispute settlement beyond the Security Council. He said Pakistan had played an important role in mediating between the United States and Iran, helping bring about a ceasefire in April, facilitating the Islamabad talks and contributing to the process that led to the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding in June. “Our leadership remains closely engaged with all sides and other friends and partners to advance the prospects of peace,” he said. On Palestine, Mr Ahmad said Pakistan had remained a “forceful voice” in the Council and played a key role in supporting the Comprehensive Plan on Gaza and Security Council Resolution 2803. The measures, he said, helped bring about a ceasefire, opened humanitarian space in Gaza and, importantly, restored a political horizon for Palestinian self-determination and statehood. Pakistan also used several Arria Formula meetings of the Security Council to focus attention on the unresolved Jammu and Kashmir dispute and the need for its peaceful settlement in accordance with international legitimacy and relevant Security Council resolutions. Published in Dawn, October 6th, 2026

Pims gets new executive director and joint executive director, notifications raise eyebrows. ISLAMABAD: After almost six weeks having passed since the fire incident , the capital’s largest hospital Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) got a new executive director (ED) and joint executive director (JED). However, the notifications raised eye brows as the charge of ED has been given to an officer who has passed his age of superannuation while the JED’s charge has been given to a contractual employee who has been working in the hospital for the last over one year. It is worth mentioning here that after the fire incident at Pims in which 14 newborn babies had died on August 26 and later the 15th baby also passed away , Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had taken notice and suspended as many as eight officers. The charge of ED was given to Dr Mohammad Salman who is also head of the National Institute of Health (NIH). According to two notifications, available with Dawn , in pursuance of the directives of the Prime Minister’s Office, Prof Dr Tanwir Khaliq currently posted as vice chancellor, Shaheed Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto Medical University (SZABMU), Islamabad has been assigned the additional charge of the post of executive director (BPS-21), Pims, in addition to his own duties for a period of three months or till the availability of regular incumbent of the post, whichever is earlier. “The officer will be entitled to draw additional remuneration as admissible under the rules. Dr. Mohammad Salman presently working as executive director (BPS-21), Pims, Islamabad is hereby repatriated to his parent department and directed to resume his duties on same positions in NIH, Islamabad with immediate effect,” the notification reads. The second notification states: “With the approval of the competent authority i.e. Secretary, Ministry of Health, Prof. Dr. Brig. (Retd.) Azmat Hayat, Professor of Electrophysiology, Pims, Islamabad is hereby assigned additional charge of the post of Joint Executive Director (BPS-20/Medical), Pims, in addition to his own duties for a period of three months or till the availability of regular incumbent of the post, whichever is earlier. The officer will be entitled to draw additional remuneration as admissible under the rules.” A senior doctor of the hospital, wishing not to be named, said Dr Tanwir Khaliq had retired almost six years ago. “Now additional charge of the hospital head has been given to him. We (doctors) cannot understand that how he will handle two jobs,” he asked. “Prof. Dr. Brig. (Retd.) Azmat Hayat was working in Pims as a contractual employee in MP-II scale. Now he has got the position of JED in the hospital. I don’t remember if a contractual employee got such position in the past,” he said. Published in Dawn, October 6th, 2026

Punajb CM Maryam receives UN-Habitat award. Last ruler of Khairpur State passes away. SUKKUR: Mir Ali Murad Khan Talpur, the last ruler of the former princely state of Khairpur, passed away here on Monday. He was 93. He has left behind two sons and a daughter. The funeral prayers will be offered at Kot Diji on Tuesday (today) at 11am. The late Talpur played a significant role in the history of Khairpur State during the transition following the creation of Pakistan. Tens of thousands expected in Paris for high school protests. Tens of thousands of demonstrators are expected on the streets of Paris on Tuesday as France’s powerful trade unions join high school students rallying for better conditions in a wave of protests marked by clashes with police. Students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds since late September, complaining of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures. While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have lit dustbin fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police, who have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds. French high school students gather outside the Lycee Charles Peguy high school in Paris as part of a nationwide day of demonstrations and blockades, France, October 6, 2026. —Reuters The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement, with a 15-year-old losing a hand on Monday after, according to a police union source, he picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot officers. The unrest has erupted with just months to go before the 2027 election to choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron after his maximum two terms in office. More protests are expected across the country on Tuesday after teaching was disrupted at 589 of the country’s 3,700 lycees and 32 universities, according to the education ministry and a student union. Authorities are expecting some 20,000 to 40,000 demonstrators in Paris. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office has called for “peaceful” gatherings, calling for a return to “a structured, legal and democratic form of opposition”. The head of the CGT labour union, Sophie Binet, has said its members would be there to “protect high school students”. ‘Disproportionate police repression’ Several unions and rights groups have accused the police of using disproportionate force against the protesters. Amnesty International late Monday said the French authorities should “put an end to the disproportionate police repression seen in recent days during student protests”. “The images and testimonies widely circulated over the past week raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of tear gas, batons and policing techniques by the police,” Amnesty’s Anne Savinel-Barras said. The police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late Monday. The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of being behind the movement. Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods. Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education ministry. More than 5,000 people, 87 per cent of them minors, have been arrested. French high school students gather outside the Lycee Charles Peguy high school in Paris as part of a nationwide day of demonstrations and blockades, voicing anger over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings, which students blame on years of underinvestment, France, October 6, 2026. —Reuters Lecornu’s office said 85 teaching staff have also been injured. The prime minister has sought to address the issue of missing teachers and renovating buildings that are dilapidated. The government is also pushing legislation to make those responsible for damaging public property pay for repairs themselves, instead of using public funds. Lecornu has said the draft law could allow compensation payments to be recovered from family allowances and housing benefits while ensuring a minimum income. Union leader Binet has said it would “end up targeting the most vulnerable families”.

Security forces kill 5 terrorists in North Waziristan IBO: state media. Security forces on Tuesday killed five terrorists in an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in North Waziristan, state broadcaster Radio Pakistan reported. Two terrorists were injured in the operation, it said. Forces targeted hideouts of the terrorists, who belonged to Fitna al-Khawarij , according to security sources. Fitna al Khawarij is a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday commended the security forces for the successful IBO. “The timely and effective actions of the security forces are playing an important role in foiling the nefarious designs of terrorist elements,” President Zardari said in his statement. According to the state broadcaster, PM Shehbaz reaffirmed that operations against terrorism would continue until its complete elimination. He further said that the complete eradication of terrorism and sustainable peace under Azm-i-Istehkam vision was the government’s top priority. KP has been witnessing terrorist attacks and security challenges for a long time. The province, excluding the merged districts, recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August compared with 36 in July, representing an increase of 50 per cent, according to data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). On October 2, security forces killed seven terrorists in an IBO in North Waziristan. On September 30, security forces killed three terrorists in an IBO in KP’s Mir Ali. A day before that, in an IBO in KP’s Bara area, security forces killed five terrorists. On Monday, four terrorists were killed during an IBO in Dera Ismail Khan. On Sept 26, a dozen people lost their lives while 35 others were injured in a suicide blast that targeted the Aman Mela police checkpost in DI Khan’s Darazinda tehsil. On Sept 18, a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation . Earlier that month, over 20 terrorists were killed during multiple engagements in KP between Sept 3 and 5.

India opposition leader Rahul Gandhi briefly detained during protest seeking election chief’s resignation. India’s opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained by police on Tuesday during a march protesting against the Election Commission, demanding its chief resign and alleging wrongdoing during a revision of voter rolls. An AFP reporter saw Gandhi, a leader of the Congress Party, standing on a police barricade and waving an Indian flag. Officers detained him briefly, along with other lawmakers, and then released them soon after. Opposition parties began their march from parliament towards to the Election Commission of India (ECI), but were stopped by heavy police deployments. Some politicians sat down on the street to wait. Protests began on Friday, demanding that commission chief Gyanesh Kumar step down. Opposition politicians have accused the commission of acting at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BPJ). The ECI has rejected allegations of wrongdoing, saying the revision process is aimed at ensuring the accuracy and integrity of electoral rolls. Kumar has not commented publicly. “Gyanesh, it’s done, bro,” placards read, as well as signs alleging electoral manipulation. Parties opposing Prime Minister Narendra Modi and members of the popular ‘cockroach’ youth movement launched protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar appointed by Modi’s government after the Indian Express newspaper reported divisions in the poll body last month. Members of the Rapid Action Force (RAF), along with police officers, stand next to barricades as they prepare for a protest organised by opposition parties demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar near Parliament in New Delhi, India, October 6, 2026. —Reuters The protests mark a fresh political challenge to Modi, midway into his third term in office and just months after similar protests forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks. The reported differences over the lists and voter registration procedures stoked concern about the commission’s neutrality. Holding a large banner that said “Save Democracy”, lawmakers raised slogans against Modi and demanded that Kumar resign as they marched from parliament to the Election Commission of India headquarters in central Delhi. Supporters gather behind a barricade during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar organised by the Shiv Sena (UBT) and the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) in Mumbai, India, October 4, 2026. —Reuters “The election commission is a puppet in the hands of the government. We are fighting to save our democracy,” Mallikarjun Kharge, president of the main opposition Congress party, told reporters as the march began. Hundreds of security personnel, including paramilitaries in fatigues, fanned out in the area, with barricades thrown up and several routes closed. Television showed security personnel, some holding batons, outside the barricaded Election Commission office. Congress and other parties allege that the revised voter lists benefit Modi and his party. Kumar has not commented on the issue, but the commission and Modi’s BJP denied the accusations. Authorities advised against travel around planned protest areas and shut off some routes. Supporters gather behind a barricade during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar organised by the Shiv Sena (UBT) and the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) in Mumbai, India, October 4, 2026. —Reuters Tuesday’s event is the latest of a series of almost daily demonstrations by student organisations, political parties and the ‘cockroach’ movement, which began last week. India’s Supreme Court agreed on Monday to hear legal arguments seeking its intervention in the accusations against the poll body’s voter drive, and the conduct of its chief. If “there are decisions against the law … We will take care of it,” the court said at the hearing, after the petitioners alleged bias by the poll body.

BISE Bannu, DI Khan postpone this week’s exams, citing suspension of communication services. BANNU: The Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education (BISE) Bannu has postponed the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) Annual-II/Oriental Languages Examination 2026 papers scheduled for October 7, 8, 9 and 10 due to the security situation in the region. According to a notification issued by the BISE Bannu chairman on October 3, the decision was taken in view of the prevailing security situation and the suspension of mobile phone and internet services within the board’s jurisdiction. The board said the suspension of communication services could cause serious inconvenience to students, parents, teachers and examination administration, particularly in the timely receipt and dissemination of roll numbers, duty letters and other examination-related communications. It could also affect the dispatch of examination stationery to examination centres. The notification said the prevailing circumstances could adversely affect the smooth and transparent conduct of the examinations. However, all remaining examinations will be held according to the notified date sheet, the board clarified. The postponed papers will be rescheduled later, and a revised schedule will be issued separately by BISE Bannu. The decision applies to the board’s jurisdiction, comprising Bannu, Lakki Marwat and North Waziristan. All heads of institutions, supervisory staff, candidates and other stakeholders have been directed to take note of the decision and ensure its immediate dissemination. According to Controller Examinations Qaiser Anwar, the examinations will now commence on Oct 12. Mobile phone services in DI Khan have been suspended for three days. KP has been facing security challenges, and according to monthly data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), KP experienced a “particularly sharp increase in the lethality of militant violence” in September. Punjab extends ban on gatherings until Oct 15, citing ‘threats of terrorist activity’. LAHORE: The Punjab government on Tuesday extended Section 144 across the province for 10 days until October 15 amid threats of terrorist activities, according to a notification issued by the provincial home department. The development comes as the previous 13-day period expired on Oct 5. The restrictions have been in place across Punjab since September. According to a notification issued by the Punjab Home Department on Oct 6, a copy of which is available with Dawn, the restrictions will remain in force for 10 days from the date of issuance unless modified or withdrawn earlier. The notification outlined the restrictions as follows: Assemblies, processions and gatherings of five or more people have been banned in any public place, street, road, highway, motorway or open space. Inciting people to participate in an unlawful assembly has also been prohibited. The carrying, display or brandishing of all kinds of weapons in public places was banned as well, except law enforcement, intelligence, and security agencies performing official duties. The ban on gatherings is not applicable to marriage ceremonies, funeral prayers, burial gatherings and prayers in mosques and churches, official duties of government or semi-government organisations, courts of law and other events permitted by the deputy commissioner concerned under Section 16 of the Punjab Civil Administration Act, 2017. The notification cited “credible reports” indicating “a serious and imminent threat to public peace, tranquillity and the safety of life and property across Punjab from terrorist organisations and hostile intelligence agencies”. It said multiple “threat alerts” had been received regarding possible terrorist activities being planned by hostile agencies, involving suicide bombers, vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices and target killings during large public gatherings. “Such activities could create mayhem and social unrest and disrupt public peace and tranquillity,” the notification read. “Assemblies of people, rallies, gatherings, sit-ins, processions, demonstrations and jalsas could present potential targets for terrorist attacks, and the possibility of an untoward incident or act of terrorism could not be ruled out during such activities,” it added. The notification further said there was also strong apprehension that certain elements could engage in activities likely to result in assemblies of people, making them easy targets for hostile activity by terrorists or terrorist organisations. The development comes amid PTI’s long march, which the party went ahead with despite warnings from the Centre. The protest aims to demand the release of jailed party founder and former prime minister Imran Khan. Ahead of the protest, similar restrictions have been imposed in other parts of the country recently. Section 144 was also imposed in Karachi last month, with authorities banning gatherings of more than five people in the city until Sept 30. Movement on several roads in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Dera Ismail Khan, Upper and Lower South Waziristan, Tank and Hangu was also restricted under Section 144 for varying periods. A similar ban was imposed in Islamabad for two months, while gatherings in the federal capital are also banned under the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act 2024 , which had been rushed through the National Assembly. The Balochistan government has also imposed Section 144 throughout the province for 30 days, citing reports indicating the likelihood of activities and gatherings that could adversely affect law and order and the safety and security of the public.

Kenya confirms first Ebola case imported from Congo, patient has died. Kenya has recorded its first confirmed Ebola case, a Kenyan citizen who has been living in Democratic Republic of Congo and arrived in Nairobi on Saturday, Health Minister Aden Duale said. The patient has since died, and 28 contacts have been identified so far including family members and health workers, Duale told a press conference. So far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”, he said. The man, who has not been named, fell ill around a month ago and had been treated in the DRC, Duale told reporters, before travelling overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, and then flying to Nairobi on October 3. He added that he was screened and confirmed positive for the deadly virus, saying that the man “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130”. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” Duale added. Kenya has previously never recorded an Ebola case and Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year for the creation of an Ebola facility at Laikipia Air Base, about 200 kilometres from Nairobi. Congo has been battling its largest-ever Ebola outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species. The outbreak was declared in mid-May but may have started months earlier and has so far resisted containment efforts, with the Central African country recording more than 8,000 cases and over 4,000 deaths. The outbreak earlier spread to Uganda, which reported 20 cases and two deaths, but the World Health Organisation declared Uganda free of the disease in August. The disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, living or dead. It can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.

4 FBR officials, traffic policeman martyred in DI Khan attacks: police.
