On Sept 27 , 14 people, including two rescue officials, were martyred and 35 sustained injuries after a suicide bomber rammed an explosive-laden vehicle into a police checkpost in and then targeted an ambulance taking bodies to hospital in DI Khan. On Sept 18, a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation .

Nobel physics prize honours work on 'ghost messengers from space'. Belgian physicist Francis Halzen on Tuesday won the Nobel Prize in Physics for work on subatomic particles at the South Pole, the award jury said. “This year’s prize is about ghostly messengers from space,” Ellen Moons, secretary general of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a news conference. Halzen was honoured “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”, the jury said. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences noted that Halzen’s “vision and scientific leadership” had been fundamental for the observatory, which it described as “a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors”. Using the observatory, researchers can capture neutrinos — rare subatomic particles — “from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe”. “This Nobel Prize is about a giant ice cube positioned at the South Pole of our globe. The ice cube enables the detection of neutrinos,” professor Eva Olsson, a member of the Nobel Committee for Physics, told reporters. Halzen, 82, was born in Tienen, Belgium and is a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the United States. “It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” he told the news conference by telephone shortly after the prize was announced. “But it’s a great pleasure to hear about this prize,” Halzen said. The award is the second Nobel of the season, after the Medicine Prize was awarded on Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel. The researchers were honoured for their pioneering work in the field of optogenetics, which involves controlling nerve signals with light. Peace prize lobbying Last year, the Nobel Prize in Physics went to Briton John Clarke, Frenchman Michel Devoret and American John Martinis for putting quantum mechanics into action and enabling the development of all kinds of digital technology from cellphones to a new generation of computers. The physics prize will be followed by the chemistry one on Wednesday. The literature laureate will be revealed on Thursday, with some pundits suggesting that the Swedish Academy could follow up last year’s award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a woman writer, possibly from Latin America. The perhaps most keenly anticipated award — the peace prize — is due on Friday. US President Donald Trump lobbied intensively last year to get the prize — and Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado ended up giving him her Nobel medal — and the committee is aware he will be watching closely again. The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12. The Nobel consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a 12-million-kronor ($1.2 million) prize sum, which is shared if there is more than one winner in a discipline. The laureates will receive their prizes at a formal ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.

Al-Qadir Trust case: PTI lawyers approach FCC for early hearing of Bushra Bibi’s appeal. ISLAMABAD: Senior members of the PTI legal team on Tuesday approached the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) seeking early fixation of a criminal appeal filed by former first lady Bushra Bibi in the £190 million Al-Qadir Trust case . The former first lady was handed a seven-year sentence in the case in January last year, and is currently imprisoned at Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail. The court found Imran and Bushra guilty of giving undue favours to property tycoon Malik Riaz in retrieving his laundered money from the United Kingdom. Bushra, along with Imran, had initially moved the Islamabad High Court (IHC) for the suspension of her sentence in July last year. But the high court dismissed their requests in May 2026, observing that their appeals against their convictions had already been fixed for hearing. On Tuesday, led by PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja and Barrister Salman Safdar, the lawyers requested the court office to fix the criminal appeal for an early hearing before an appropriate bench of the top court. The court office assured the delegation that the appeal would be numbered within the week and fixed for hearing accordingly, Advocate Intezar Hussain Panjutha told Dawn. He said no fresh application was filed on Tuesday, though a verbal request was made for early registration and fixation of the case. Earlier, Barrister Salman Safdar had filed an application before the FCC on Sept 17, citing a rapidly deteriorating ocular condition that threatened the appellant’s remaining eyesight. The application said Bushra’s role, as attributed by the prosecution, was confined to aiding and abetting and did not involve any primary or substantive act constituting the gravamen of the offence. It said the applicant was 54 years old and had been convicted under Section 9(a)(xii) of the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999, for aiding and abetting. The application also argued that Bushra was a woman and that it was a settled practice, consistent with the spirit of the first proviso to Section 497(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, that female litigants, particularly those in custody, be heard on a priority basis. It regretted that she had already suffered “grave and irreversible prejudice” because of prolonged proceedings before the IHC, where, during the pendency of her application for suspension of sentence, she developed a serious ocular condition and underwent surgery on one eye on April 16, 2026. “She continues to face a real risk to her remaining eye,” the application said, citing further medical examinations and the details contained in a synopsis report submitted by the superintendent of Central Jail Adiala before the Supreme Court. According to the report, Bushra was diagnosed with Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD) in her right eye. She subsequently developed a “black curtain” and acute deterioration, was declared an ocular emergency and underwent surgery at Al-Shifa Trust Eye Hospital. A later examination in jail revealed new opacity and PVD in progress in her previously unaffected left eye, the application said. “The continued delay in fixation directly imperils the applicant’s health and eyesight,” it said, adding that the deterioration already suffered was demonstrably linked to the delay before the IHC. The application contended that, taking into account the proceedings before the IHC and the FCC, Bushra’s application/appeal against the dismissal of her suspension-of-sentence plea had remained undecided for approximately 19 months. It said the application was confined to the “limited question of delay” in adjudication of her request for suspension of sentence and did not require the FCC to undertake a detailed examination of the merits of the main appeal. The application requested the FCC to dispose of the matter through a short hearing and fix the appeal for hearing in the week commencing Sept 21, “in the interest of justice”.

Mass surveillance. THE new National Cybercrime Investigation Agency chief, Ali Nasir Rizvi, has adopted a “zero-tolerance policy against fake news and anti-state propaganda”, according to the agency. Troublingly, neither ‘fake news’ nor ‘anti-state propaganda’ has a clear, legal meaning, and the fact that these terms are now centrepieces in the NCCIA’s policy gives rise to concerns about what the state’s priorities truly are. The authority’s mandate includes protecting citizens from fraud, harassment, blackmail, and financial scams. It recently shut down several fraudulent call centres , showing it can deliver well on those responsibilities. Monitoring and policing opinion are something else altogether. Further, the fact that the NCCIA has established ‘cyber patrolling units’ in every region is alarming. Why is the authority engaging in mass public surveillance? What is being monitored, for what purpose, and under what legal authority? Who will be providing oversight, and how will citizens be protected from excessive surveillance? Since the DG has promised merit and transparency, he should satisfy the public in this regard. It is worth pointing out here that these special units for surveillance sit atop the 2025 Peca amendments , which criminalised spreading ‘false’ information, amid strong protests from journalists and rights groups. The timing of the announcement also comes amidst a deadlock between the government and the opposition over protests announced by the latter. In such a charged political environment, the message would seem to be that dissent, not disinformation, is the actual target. It is hoped that the NCCIA will act with restraint and transparency to avoid cementing that perception. The authority must avoid politicising its work. Misinformation and disinformation do real harm; the answer to them is fast, credible official communication, improved media literacy, and platform accountability, not prosecution and lawfare. The state must build trust with the public if it wishes to defeat what it calls ‘fake news’ and ‘propaganda’. Published in Dawn, October 6th, 2026

Taps run dry in Karachi's Clifton, Defence as official tanker service faces delays. KARACHI: Residents of Clifton and Defence, who rely on water tankers, have been facing difficulty in getting a bowser from the Cantonment Board Clifton (CBC) as its tanker service is facing delays due to an acute shortage. At a recent meeting between the CBC and the Clifton Defence Community (CDC), a detailed discussion was held on the acute water shortage faced by the residents, a Rs14 billion project to lay a new waterline dedicated from Dumlottee to DHA and pending tanker supply applications. When many residents, who attended the meeting, complained that they are not even getting water through the CBC tankers despite having been given out tokens, it was explained that owing to the current shortage, the tanker supply is two to three months behind schedule. The residents suggested that the Karachi Water and Sewerage Corporation water tankers be diverted to DHA too to take care of the backlog in supplying water as they are also available at a relatively lower price than the private tankers and can be booked a few days in advance. In meeting with residents, CBC officials attribute backlog in bowser supply to water shortage In a bid to learn more about the proposed dedicated waterline project, CDC President Abdur Rehman inquired about its progress from CBC officials, including Secretary Sajjad Nazir and Chief Cantonment Engineer Abdul Rahim Shaikh. It was explained that work on the new pipeline, expected to complete in a year’s time, has already started. The pipeline will carry unfiltered water from Dumlottee, which will then be purified through filtration plants before being supplied to the residents through their lines. The residents also requested that the existing water distribution system be improved before the new project is completed. There were other complaints also raised by residents about private tankers filling up from CBC hydrants to which the CBC officials denied any such action. They further said that if any resident saw a private tanker filling water from a CBC hydrant, they should take a picture of it and immediately send it to the CBC officials concerned so that the matter can be investigated and necessary action be taken. “There are unnecessary and redundant lines and ineffective management of valves that need to be looked into,” said CDC’s President Abdur Rehman. He also highlighted the residents’ suggestion of installing water meters and devising an effective system for supply according to water consumption, so that the internal system is fully ready by the time the water supply from the new line begins. Regarding residents’ concerns over tanker service delays, CBC Secretary Nazir told Dawn: “We facilitated those [residents] at the meeting who showed us their tokens [for water tankers] on a priority basis the very same day.” Published in Dawn, October 6th, 2026

Russia denies imposing anti-plague measures after death of worker. Russian authorities denied Tuesday that they were imposing special anti-plague measures after a laboratory technician reportedly died of the disease, as the UN’s health agency said the risk to the country was low. It was reported last week that a worker at an anti-plague institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk region died of pneumonic plague. But the authorities say the cause of death is not confirmed and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor has denied claims circulating in a document online that special measures had been put in place. “We wish to clarify that the document and information in question do not originate from official sources and are untrue,” it said on Telegram. “No such decisions have been made at this time,” it said, stressing that the health situation in the region was stable. Russian news outlet People of Baikal claimed on Friday that the dead woman — named as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova — may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube. Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility. The People of Baikal outlet also claimed that up to 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine. ‘Low risk’ But Russian officials said postmortem tests had not detected the disease. Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that a Rospotrebnadzor watchdog inspection had found that the woman died of pneumonia and the cause was “undetermined”. “No microorganisms linked to the young woman’s professional work were found in her biological samples,” he said. And there had been “no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention” since the death, he added. Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas. Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). “The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk,” WHO spokesman Christian Lindmeier told a press briefing in Geneva. He said the risk was low for Russia as a whole, and very low for the rest of Europe. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said his government was [looking at the situation](https:// . @SecRubio on the possible Russia plague outbreak: "We’re watching and monitoring it closely. I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus." https://t.co/pWbvfmV6uE — Rapid Response 47 ( @RapidResponse47 ) October 5, 2026 ) “very strongly”. “We’ll help them as much as we can,” he told reporters on Monday when asked about the situation. An international conference on plague and other infectious diseases will meanwhile be held in Irkutsk on October 21-22. The conference was arranged in June and organisers said it was “unrelated to the recent death of an employee of the anti-plague institute”.

PTI long march won’t be allowed beyond Attock, warns Kundi. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi on Tuesday vowed that PTI’s long march would not be allowed to proceed beyond Attock in Punjab — which borders KP — saying the party “did not have the capacity” to do so. The opposition has gone ahead with its march despite warnings from the Centre, which has vowed to prevent any gatherings in Islamabad. The protest aims to demand the release of jailed party founder and former prime minister Imran Khan. PTI decided to embark on the march after weekend talks with the federal government to bridge their differences failed for multiple reasons , particularly over the counterterrorism policy. So far, the KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi-led convoy has aimed to reach Khairabad — which borders Punjab — by October 8, where the KP chief minister will announce the next plan of action. Kundi made the remarks while speaking to Geo News programme ‘Geo Pakistan’. “They cannot go any further than Attock,” Kundi said, challenging PTI to “try to take a step”. He contended that the party did not have “enough capacity” to march further. “They claim to have two million people with them […] show us the people; they don’t have the capacity.” Kundi said the province was suffering from terrorism and “yet, they [PTI] want to march to Islamabad instead”. Speaking about his recent meeting with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi in Peshawar, the governor recalled that the two often held meetings to discuss the security situation, and during last week’s meeting, the two also discussed “dialogue with the PTI as well as the way forward in relation to PTI’s long march”. Kundi cautioned: “If there is a mishap during the long march — especially if someone from southern KP who wants to reach Islamabad to carry out a plot [is involved] — what screening mechanisms does PTI have in place to prevent that from happening?” He also assailed the PTI-led KP government for “staying silent” on terrorist incidents. “When the federal government asks for their support against militancy, they say that the army should leave the province and that we should hold a dialogue with Afghanistan,” Kundi said, accusing the incarcerated PTI founder of “having militants settled in KP in the past”. “He was called Taliban Khan,” Kundi added, referring to Imran. Kundi further claimed that KP Chief Minister Afridi was taking “directions from PTI leader Murad Saeed”, whom the governor described as a “runaway”. He vowed that Saeed “will be brought before the people and made to pay for his actions”. Speaking about the possibility of governor’s rule in KP, Kundi said: “If the president and prime minister hand the task to the province […] and deem governor’s rule necessary, the province will ensure its implementation.” He held that governor’s rule was the last resort. “Surgery is the last option; first, you are put on medication. No one wishes to do it,” he said, referring to governor’s rule. “We want to continue, but if you are pushed to the limit and there is no option left, then it is considered.” On Monday night, after reaching Kohat’s Lachi tehsil, CM Afridi said while addressing PTI supporters that this time, the party’s struggle was a long one that required endurance and sustained mobilisation, according to a statement issued by his office. “We must not exhaust ourselves. Our struggle is a long one,” he said, adding that, however, from Oct 8 onwards, a “T20 match” would begin. The convoy stayed overnight in Kohat and plans to resume the journey today towards Peshawar at 3pm. On the afternoon of Oct 7, the caravan will depart from Budh Bair in Peshawar and spend the night near Charsadda Interchange. The protesters will then move forward the next afternoon and spend the night of Oct 8 at Khairabad. Notably, the KP CM has refrained from detailing the final leg of the trip to the federal capital and said the plan for the next phase would be announced at Khairabad. The march so far After launching the already-postponed march from Lakki Marwat on Sunday afternoon, the KP CM’s caravan reached Karak at night, where Afridi addressed supporters at Jail Chowk. Ahead of the march, movement on several roads in KP’s Dera Ismail Khan, Upper and Lower South Waziristan, Tank and Hangu was restricted under Section 144 for varying periods . On Sunday, former KP CM Ali Amin Gandapur, who was leading PTI workers from DI Khan to Lakki Marwat, took a U-turn from Yarik because of road blockades and the prevailing law and order situation. Noting that Section 144 had been imposed in the area for three days, Gandapur stressed that the party leadership had clearly directed workers not to damage public property or engage in any activity that could worsen the situation. Nevertheless, he contended that the return should not be viewed as a withdrawal from the protest movement, but as a temporary decision. In Karachi , a planned protest campaign in different areas was disrupted after police deployed personnel at several locations, blocked roads and detained several party workers and leaders. The PTI claimed that police detained more than 75 of its leaders and workers, including women, from different parts of Karachi. It further alleged that arrests made in other parts of Sindh, including Sukkur, put the total number of detained PTI workers across the province at more than 100. On Saturday night, an opposition delegation comprising PTI and Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP), and a joint team of the government and PPP held hours-long negotiations , which ended in a deadlock. While the federal government blamed CM Afridi for the failure of negotiations, PTI denied the allegations and claimed that access to Imran, his medical treatment and the federal government’s counterterrorism policy were the key reasons. According to PTI, the government agreed to restore meetings between Imran and his family members and lawyers from Tuesday, but “declined to make access to Imran Khan part of the proposed agreement”.

UN chief hails Pakistan's 'pivotal role' in US-Iran conflict, calls for 'return to diplomacy'. United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday lauded Pakistan’s “pivotal role” in mediating between the United States and Iran as he called on the parties to end the conflict and return to diplomacy. Addressing a press conference in Islamabad alongside Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, he said: “Pakistan’s spirit of engagement is front and centre on issues of international peace and security. “I salute Pakistan’s leadership for helping to create the conditions for dialogue between the US and Iran and mediating that conflict. Your efforts helped deliver the Islamabad memorandum of understanding , the subsequent ceasefire and the framework for future negotiations . Every Pakistani should be proud of that pivotal role,” he said. “And from Islamabad, I want to send a loud and clear message to all parties: end the conflict, return to diplomacy and restore navigational rights in accordance with international law. There will never be peace in the region until the right of self-determination of the Palestinian people is recognised, as Pakistan has long championed,” he said. At the outset of his speech, the UN chief said that it was “wonderful to be back in Pakistan”. “I am in the closing months of my tenure as UN secretary general. Before that, I served ten years as UN high commissioner for refugees,” he said. “Pakistan has shown that, even in difficult circumstances, perhaps especially in difficult circumstances, compassion and responsibility must go hand-in-hand,” he said. He asserted that Pakistan mattered not only because of its size, but because it brought an “essential perspective” to global debates. “For decades, Pakistan opened its doors to millions of Afghans fleeing conflict and instability. Communities around this country shared whatever they had with people seeking protection and safety,” Guterres said. He added that the UN was committed to working together with the country to uphold protection principles and ensure that returns of Afghans “proceed in a voluntary, safe and dignified way”. According to the UN chief, Pakistan had put a spotlight on the value of multilateralism, dialogue, mediation and diplomacy at a time of growing division and mistrust around the world. “Those same values are vital within societies as well,” he stated. “Here and around the world, we know that inclusive institutions, respect for human rights, and a vibrant civic space are necessary to help strengthen social cohesion, build trust and enable people to contribute fully to their country’s future.” Guterres also appreciated Pakistan’s contributions to United Nations peacekeeping. “Pakistani women and men have served with courage and distinction in some of the most difficult and dangerous environments,” he said. “More than 180 brave Pakistani souls gave their lives in the service of peace. We honour their sacrifice.” The chief highlighted Pakistan’s leadership with Denmark on UN Security Council (UNSC) resolution 2823, which strengthened accountability for crimes against UN peacekeepers. One hundred and fifty-three countries co-sponsored the resolution, which according to Guterres, was the largest number of co-sponsors for a UNSC resolution in UN history. The UN chief also shared his plans to visit United Nations Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan (UNMOGIP) later in the day to pay tribute to the mission and to peacekeepers worldwide. Commenting on terrorism in the country, he said: “Pakistan has endured immense suffering. Thousands of people lost their lives. Families and communities across the country continue to bear scars. We stand with Pakistan in confronting this threat of terrorism.” He added that addressing terrorism and legitimate security concerns was necessary and indispensable. “Experience shows that the strongest and most effective security responses are those grounded in international law, human rights and the rule of law.” Towards the end of his speech, Guterres spoke about the climate crisis. “My last visit to Pakistan came during the catastrophic floods of 2022. I will never forget the utter devastation I saw,” he said, referring to the unprecedented floods four years ago that affected approximately 33 million people and claimed the lives of 1,700 people. “But I also saw the resilience, determination and solidarity of the Pakistani people,” Guterres said. “Pakistan is on the frontlines of climate chaos despite contributing only a tiny fraction of global emissions.” He appreciated Pakistan’s response to the crises, including establishment of the Loss and Damage Fund and the country’s growing clean energy transition. However, he asserted that leadership from vulnerable developing countries cannot substitute for responsibility from developed countries. “The G20 represents 80 per cent of global emissions. We need a drastic reduction in those emissions this decade,” he highlighted. “The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities must apply, but all countries must do their part,” he said. Meanwhile, Dar said he “greatly appreciated” Guterres’ visit, which he asserted was a reflection of the “long-standing and close cooperation” between Pakistan and the UN. “It also shows our common resolve to strengthen multilateralism and our cooperation at a time of profound global challenges,” he said. “We have consistently sought to uphold the purposes and principles of the UN charter, advance international peace and security, contribute to peacekeeping and strengthen multilateral solutions to global challenges.” Dar referred to Guterres as a “great friend” of Pakistan, adding that the country would not forget his solidarity during the 2022 floods as well as his efforts to mobilise international support for recovery and reconstruction. During its time as an elected member of the UNSC, Dar said Pakistan had tried to make “significant contributions” to international peace and security, with particular emphasis on dialogue, diplomacy, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. “Our initiative on resolution 2788 on strengthening multilateralism and mechanisms for the peaceful settlement of disputes is a reflection of Pakistan’s approach in this regard,” the minister recalled. “The unanimous adoption of that resolution reaffirmed the importance of negotiation, mediation, preventive diplomacy, and the good offices of the UN secretary general.” He appreciated Guterres’ engagement with the follow-up to the resolution, including the participation and presentation of “solid recommendations” in the open debate held in July this year. Dar said the country valued the secretary general’s “readiness” to extend his good offices in situations where dialogue and diplomacy could help reduce tensions and create space for peaceful solutions. “This is particularly relevant at a time when the international community is confronted with multiple conflicts and crises,” he reiterated. “Pakistan believes that the UN must remain at the centre of international efforts to address these challenges and that diplomacy must be given every opportunity to succeed.” Pakistan, Dar said, had played a “proactive and constructive” role in promoting dialogue and de-escalation in the Gulf region. He appreciated Guterres’ support for Pakistan’s mediation efforts and his recognition of the importance of diplomatic engagement. “Pakistan’s role in facilitating dialogue is consistent with our broader approach at the UN, which is to promote cooperation over confrontation, dialogue over conflict and peaceful settlement over the use of force,” he stated. The minister said Pakistan supported the chief’s UN80 initiative, which seeks to make the UN more “effective, efficient and fit for purpose”. “We believe that efforts to strengthen the organisation must reinforce its ability to deliver on its core mandates, while ensuring that the priorities and concerns of developing countries remain central.” According to him, stronger, effective, inclusive, and representative multilateralism was needed at a time of growing geopolitical tensions, conflicts, humanitarian crises, climate vulnerabilities and economic pressures. He further appreciated the UN chief’s “continued attention” to issues of particular importance to Pakistan, including regional peace and stability, counter-terrorism, climate vulnerability and development challenges. “We also greatly appreciate the UN’s consistent position on the Jammu and Kashmir dispute and the reiteration of the UN framework and UNSC resolutions for resolving the dispute,” he said. Dar said he briefed the UN chief on India’s unilateral move of holding the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance , which he referred to as a blatant violation of international law. “We underscored the need to ensure that India stops weaponising water and fulfils its obligations under the IWT.” He also highlighted Pakistan’s “deep concern” at the continued use of Afghan soil for carrying out terrorist attacks against Pakistan. He urged the UN chief and the international community to help address these challenges. Dar meets UN chief Earlier in the day, Dar held a one-on-one meeting with the UN chief, with the two discussing regional and global issues relating to peace and security, the Foreign Office (FO) said. The FO said the discussions covered Palestine, Jammu and Kashmir, Afghanistan, counter-terrorism and the future of multilateralism. Dar briefed the UN secretary general on Pakistan’s positions on Jammu and Kashmir and the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), reaffirming Islamabad’s call for a just and peaceful resolution of the Kashmir dispute in accordance with relevant UNSC resolutions. According to the FO, Dar also highlighted Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts to promote dialogue and de-escalation, including its facilitation of the Islamabad talks between the US and Iran. He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to dialogue and diplomacy as the most effective means of resolving disputes. The UN secretary general appreciated Pakistan’s longstanding contribution to the UN, as well as its diplomatic efforts to promote dialogue, mediation and de-escalation, the FO said. Guterres arrived in Islamabad in the early hours of Tuesday for a two-day official visit. “Upon arrival, the secretary-general was received by Acting Foreign Secretary Ambassador Nabeel Munir,” the FO said in a post on X. The visit comes as Guterres’ 10-year tenure as UN chief is set to end on Dec 31. During the visit, Guterres is set to meet President Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, the FO said on Monday. The UN chief is also scheduled to visit the headquarters of the UNMOGIP and attend a briefing at the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) headquarters. In its Monday statement, the FO said that during Guterres’ visit, Pakistan’s “efforts towards strengthening multilateralism and international peace and security, as well as its strides towards disaster preparedness and early warning, will be highlighted”. PM Shehbaz met Guterres on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last month. The two discussed major regional and international developments, including the situation in the Middle East. In that meeting, Guterres commended Pakistan’s role and strong voice at the UN, as well as its contribution to international peace and security. The UN chief also appreciated Pakistan’s role and sacrifices in countering terrorism. Guterres’ first visit to Pakistan as the UN secretary general was in February 2020, about three years after he was elected to the position in 2016.

PM Shehbaz orders gas load management plan for winter, steps for ensuring uninterrupted imports. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday directed the relevant authorities to prepare a comprehensive plan for gas load management and take all necessary measures to ensure uninterrupted gas imports during the winter season, given the regional situation. He issued these instructions while chairing a meeting on gas load management during the winter season, held in Islamabad, a statement by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said. “The prime minister directed that a comprehensive plan be devised for gas load management, all necessary measures be taken in advance, an extensive public awareness campaign on the implementation of the gas load management plan be launched and all necessary steps be taken to ensure uninterrupted gas imports, keeping in view the current regional situation,” the PMO said. The meeting was also briefed on measures taken in advance for gas load management, the statement added. The participants were informed that domestic consumers would be given priority for the supply of locally produced gas while RLNG would be prioritised for power generation and industries, it said. Moreover, a public awareness campaign would be launched to promote alternative energy sources at the household level in place of locally supplied gas, according to the statement. “Measures are also being taken to ensure the uninterrupted transmission of gas from reserves in the northern regions of the country,” the PMO said, adding that a proposal to introduce bank financing facilities for electric appliances used for water and space heating was also under consideration. The meeting was attended by National Food Security Minister Rana Tanveer Hussain, Economic Affairs Minister Ahad Khan Cheema, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Industry Haroon Akhtar, Minister of State for Finance and Railways Bilal Azhar Kayani and relevant senior government officials. The meeting took place as the authorities struggle to finalise the liquefied natural gas (LNG) import plan for the upcoming three winter months — December to February — amid a challenging supply situation stemming from the US-Iran conflict. Renewed hostilities in the Middle East have resulted in disruption of major oil and gas supply routes — the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and caused fuel prices to rise. Against this backdrop, gas companies and the Petroleum Division had sought at least 22 import cargoes for the three-month period, but the task force on energy, led by Lt Gen Zafar Iqbal, has promised no more than 10-12 cargoes of around 100 million cubic feet each on a best-effort basis, using all diplomatic and logistical channels. The plan will be presented to the prime minister for approval, given the involvement of around $100m per spot cargo and the requirement for consent from the Ministry of Finance and the State Bank of Pakistan. The matter has assumed greater importance because the LNG import plan will affect the current account targets agreed upon by the Ministry of Finance and the International Monetary Fund, whose staff mission is c urrently in Pakistan and holding talks that could pave the way for the disbursement of about $1.2 billion under two concurrent programmes. Sources, meanwhile, indicate that actual LNG imports may not exceed seven to eight cargoes over the three winter months, given prevailing market conditions, which would bring the outcome closer to the Ministry of Finance’s desired level. In a related development, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) has notified an eight per cent increase in liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), raising the cost of the 11.8kg domestic cylinder by Rs244.14 for October.

PM Shehbaz urges PTI to call off long march, resolve issues through dialogue. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday urged the PTI to end its long march to Islamabad and invited the opposition to sit with the government to resolve contentious issues through political dialogue. The opposition has gone ahead with its march despite warnings from the Centre, which has vowed to prevent any gatherings in Islamabad. The protest aims to demand the release of jailed party founder and former prime minister Imran Khan. Addressing the groundbreaking ceremony of the Kashmir Chowk underpass in Islamabad on Tuesday, the premier said it was “unfortunate” that the “dreadful shadows” of long marches were hovering again, despite the PML-N and the PPP making efforts to engage the PTI in talks. The two parties, the prime minister said, held talks for two days in National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq’s chamber, and “it was hoped that politics of confrontation would end”. “Unfortunately, that did not happen. They [PTI] only had one purpose: to ensure that the talks do not succeed,” the premier said, adding that the opposition party demanded changes to things already settled upon. PM Shehbaz asserted that these protests and long marches affected the country’s economy and created hindrances in exports, imports and manufacturing. “We collectively improved the economy in 2.5 years and reached macroeconomic stability. Now is the time for it to flourish,” the premier added. “In September, our information technology exports, remittances and the country’s production improved,” he said. “If someone harms it, is it not equivalent to being an enemy of the country?” The premier stressed that putting the economy in shambles and the lives of people in danger will not be allowed. “The law will take its course,” he said. “I will still say: come to your senses. Will your actions harm the country or benefit it? … End your long march and protests. When you end them, we will surely sit down with you,” he said. Earlier in the same ceremony, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said, without naming anyone, that people had to see for themselves which public representatives were working for their welfare and which ones were engaging in “negative politics”. Tallal says talks conditional on PTI calling off march Separately, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry also spoke about the resumption of talks, saying that it remained conditional upon PTI calling off its marches and protests. Addressing a press conference in Islamabad, he warned that constitutional and political measures were in place to respond to the PTI’s ongoing long march and held Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi responsible for the breakdown in negotiations. “Political and constitutional measures are in place,” Chaudhry said. Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry speaks to media on Oct 6, 2026. — DawnNewsTV He added that the “wise” people part of the PTI’s delegation had tried to make the talks successful. Chaudhry further said that if the talks had succeeded, Pakistan would have had a united political front and the PTI would have gained “political space”. He added that a “hardening of the state” was now close, stressing that “enough softness has been shown”. “The state is like a mother, but it also has to act like a father at times,” Chaudhry said. “Constitutional options are under discussion, but the political option comes first,” he said. Commenting on the talks, Chaudhry told reporters that on the first day, Naqvi presented the government’s position regarding terrorism in KP, which included facts about the provincial government’s lack of involvement in the province’s affairs, budget and counterterrorism efforts. Chaudhry said the next day, the PTI delegation returned to Islamabad to continue talks after discussing the terms of the agreement with KP’s senior leadership in Peshawar. He said CM Afridi had previously reassured the Centre that the PTI delegation had the authority to reach an agreement on behalf of the provincial government. “We were assured that on terrorism, they [PTI] agreed 100 per cent on the federal government’s points,” Chaudhry said, adding that it was only then that Naqvi travelled to Lahore to PM Shehbaz and informed him that the PTI and the PML-N had agreed on the terrorism issue. “The prime minister said, ‘give as much political space as you can’,” Chaudhry told the media. According to him, PM Shehbaz told Naqvi that “parties’ political capital comes and goes”. Chaudhry said the premier further told Naqvi that when Pakistan was on the brink of financial default, strict measures reduced PML-N’s political capital, but they ensured that the country would not default. The second day of the talks started after the two sides had agreed on the issue of terrorism, Chaudhry said. “The win for us in the draft agreement was that we would be successful in bringing the PTI to the same page for eliminating terrorism,” he said. The draft was ready by 9pm on the second day of the talks, and Naqvi was getting ready to take it to President Asif Ali Zardari, according to the state minister. “Everything was fine,” he said, adding that some back and forth happened on further edits, but they were all agreed upon. “At the last minute, the opposition sat in a separate room for a while to consult with the KP chief minister. When they came out, they couldn’t look us in the eye and asked for permission to leave,” Chaudhry said. He added that the PTI delegation thanked the PML-N for patiently conducting the talks. The nation had agreed on the two National Action Plans (NAP) against terrorism, Chaudhry said, adding that the second plan was agreed upon during the PTI’s government under former prime minister Imran. He said that NAP was linked to “Pakistan’s Constitution, its needs, security, stability and Islamic teachings”. Citing Afridi’s statement that he wouldn’t allow a plan against the people of KP, Chaudhry questioned if Imran’s NAP was against the people of the province. Chaudhry claimed that KP was unsafe for common people and politicians alike; however, he noted that at the same time, the PTI’s leaders and workers were safe from threats in the same region. “The only one safe there is PTI,” he said, questioning, “Why do [terrorists] have a soft corner for you only?” On the possibility of talks resuming, Chaudhry said that any further talks were conditional upon the PTI calling off its marches and protests. “Don’t encourage terrorists. Instead, let’s kill them together,” Chaudhry further stated. Responding to a question about the PTI’s ongoing long march, he said, “Someone could not take over a country of 260 million people by bringing 50,000 to 100,000 people to the capital. “They are mistaken. Once their misunderstanding is cleared this time, a march won’t happen again in Pakistan,” he warned. Opp-govt dialogue failure Over the weekend, the government and opposition held two rounds of talks , which did not yield positive results, with counterterrorism policies and access to Imran emerging as two major sticking points. On Sunday, the PTI said it wanted immediate access to party chief Imran for consultations, and even agreed to forgo other demands in return for a meeting with Imran. However, the government declined to make access to Imran part of the proposed agreement, the opposition party claimed. Another deadlock was terrorism in KP. The federal government asked the KP government to support its counterterrorism measures and support emergency measures within 72 hours in the merged tribal districts, the PTI said. Instead, the PTI proposed that authorised representatives of the federal and KP governments meet within 72 hours to develop a clear, comprehensive and mutually agreed strategy for peace and counterterrorism, the statement added. The PTI said the health and medical treatment of Imran Khan was also raised as a matter of fundamental importance. Meanwhile, PTI leader Salman Akram Raja, who was a part of the opposition’s delegation, said the primary reason for the failure was disagreement on anti-terrorism actions in KP. Raja said the opposition stood firm on its principled position that anti-terrorism actions should be based on an agreement between the federal government and the KP government, and would be framed in consultation with stakeholders. After talks between the government and the opposition ended without headway, interior minister Naqvi on Sunday accused CM Afridi of “sabotaging” negotiations. On Sunday, Naqvi also held a meeting with KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi to discuss the political and security situation amid speculations of ‘imminent’ governor’s rule in the province. A government source told Dawn that the government was seriously considering the imposition of the governor’s rule in KP. But Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah said on Monday that a return to negotiations was possible if there was an assurance of positive progress by the opposition regarding counterterrorism efforts in KP. Speaking on Geo News ’ programme ‘Capital Talk’, he said that the federal government aimed to end terrorism in Pakistan, protect its borders and keep people safe. “The provincial government will have to play its role at any cost in this policy and operation,” he added. He said that both sides were still in contact, and said that if “better sense prevails” amongst the opposition and they could provide “assurance of some positive progress” in this regard, then they could sit down for more talks.

Diegograndi Special Coverage / Global 25 September 2026 8 minutes Updates from the UN General Assembly 2026 Marking the opening of the 81st UN General Assembly, Crisis Group experts discuss challenges facing the UN’s efforts to promote international peace and security. This page includes updates from the High-Level Week in New York and recent Crisis Group coverage of the UN. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy World leaders are gathering in New York during the week of 21 September for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. They will find an organisation trapped in an open-ended institutional crisis. UN diplomacy to halt wars and ease civilian suffering is largely paralysed, while a second year of cost cutting has weakened the organisation’s capacity to respond. The UN is in need of revival. Even with these limitations, the UN remains the only universal forum for international cooperation on war and peace, even as the world order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope that the next Secretary-General, set to be selected by the end of 2026, can help the organisation forge a new direction that enhances diplomacy and deepens respect for international law. A new Secretary-General, regardless of the skills and experiences that she or he may bring to the role, cannot solve the world’s crises overnight. But she or he can and should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capacities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. This special coverage page will feature all of Crisis Group’s work related to the UN General Assembly’s High-Level Week in 2026, as well as its broader work on the UN from the past year. The New Forever War mloukili Tue, 09/29/2026 - 10:38 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Middle East & North Africa 29 September 2026 1 minutes The New Forever War Originally published in Foreign Affairs Why America and Iran Fight On Without Victory Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Ali Vaez Deputy Program Director, MENA https://twitter.com/AliVaez Related Tags Iran United States When will the war in Iran end? American officials claim that the answer is soon. “I think the war is going to end immediately after the [November] election,” declared U.S. President Donald Trump in September. “They can’t hold out any longer.” Iranian leaders agree that the war’s conclusion is near. Tehran has “brought the most heavily armed army in the history of the world to its knees,” proclaimed Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, in August. Many outside analysts think that the conflict will drag on for longer and end with negotiations rather than with a clear winner. But generally, there is a sense that the fighting will soon be resolved, one way or another. Such thinking is understandable. All wars eventually end, and after months of rising energy prices, the world is especially eager for this one to stop. Yet the unsettling reality is that the conflict is nowhere near over. The war’s two principal belligerents cannot achieve their desired goals, yet they both feel they are accomplishing enough to make continued fighting through a mix of military and economic tools worth it. The United States cannot topple the Iranian regime, get it to give up its missile program, force it to abandon its nuclear program, or make it stop supporting its regional partners. But Washington can keep degrading Iran’s military and constricting its economy. Iran cannot evict the world’s only superpower from the Middle East. Yet it can keep damaging U.S. regional bases, bombing the United States’ regional allies, and disrupting international commerce. The full article can be read on the Foreign Affairs website. South Sudan’s President Jettisons Unity Government and Hardens Grip on Power eschelhaas Tue, 09/29/2026 - 11:07 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Analyst's Notebook / Africa 29 September 2026 2 minutes South Sudan’s President Jettisons Unity Government and Hardens Grip on Power Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech examines how President Kiir’s call for fresh elections aims to weaken his opponents, and may pave the way to worsening armed conflict Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Daniel Akech Senior Analyst, South Sudan https://twitter.com/jongethon Related Tags South Sudan South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir on 22 September dissolved the transitional unity government, established under a 2018 peace deal, declaring that the country would now prepare for long-delayed elections in December. But with the feasibility of holding the polls in doubt and fighting between government and rebel forces continuing in Jonglei and Upper Nile states, the move in effect serves to further concentrate power in the hands of Kiir and his family. Kiir’s move followed the adoption by parliament, which is loyal to the president, of a controversial amendment to the National Elections Act on 21 September, authorising the creation of a caretaker government. This amendment gave Kiir the opportunity to remove his five vice presidents – many of whom were appointed under the 2018 deal, including his perennial arch-rival, First Vice President Riek Machar. The government had already placed Machar, who led the rebel forces in the five-year civil war that ended in 2018, under house arrest in March last year, charging him with treason . State and rebel forces have been fighting since then, threatening to thrust South Sudan back into internecine conflict. Its last civil war is estimated to have cost nearly 400,000 lives and displaced more than four million people. President Kiir further marginalised rival factions and opposition elements in his caretaker government. His newly appointed ministers are almost entirely loyalists, whereas the Nuer – South Sudan’s second-largest ethnic group, to which Machar belongs – remain heavily underrepresented. There are now three Nuer cabinet ministers out of a total of 17, even after the president added additional appointees on 28 September. Kiir also appointed powerful figures from the security forces to become caretaker governors in key states, such as James Koang Chuol in Upper Nile, Moses Majok Gatluak in Jonglei and Rin Tueny Mabor in Lakes. Some political leaders have denounced the unrepresentative make-up of the new administration and rejected the changes. Kiir’s moves set up two potential scenarios. One is a rush to stage-manage snap elections, the first of their kind since the country’s independence in 2011, which could end up re-electing Kiir despite questions as to whether credible polls are even possible without an updated census, voter registry or dedicated funding. A mismanaged vote could also spark fresh rebellions or political violence. Alternatively, Kiir could delay elections yet again on technical grounds, effectively extending his term without the baggage of the 2018 accord’s power-sharing arrangements. Kiir is using an “inter-party dialogue” that started on 24 September to validate plans for elections in December or negotiate such an extension. Either way, Kiir’s moves have triggered alarm among the South Sudanese political elite that his aim is to consolidate power with the goal of managing a dynastic succession . His daughter Adut Kiir is now his most powerful aide, while his son Atem Salva Kiir oversees the presidential guard. Meanwhile, the new rebellion by Machar’s forces looks unlikely to subside as long as its leader remains on trial and under arrest. The U.S.-led Anti-ISIS Coalition is Leaving Iraq: What Happens Next? eschelhaas Tue, 09/29/2026 - 18:14 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iraqi security forces stand guard during a funerary procession for a slain member of Iraq's Hashed al-Shaabi, or the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), who was killed in a US-Israeli air strike in Mosul the previous evening, in Baghdad on March 8, 2026. AHMAD AL-RUBAYE / AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 29 September 2026 14 minutes The U.S.-led Anti-ISIS Coalition is Leaving Iraq: What Happens Next? The coming withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces marks a significant moment in Iraq’s tumultuous recent history. Yet with the Middle East war bringing conflict to the country and questions surrounding the state’s capacity to assert its authority, the significance is mainly symbolic. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Related Tags Iraq United States On 30 September, the U.S.-led coalition formed to fight the Islamic State (ISIS) is due to end its military mission in Iraq. While some had expected that the withdrawal of personnel and removal of materiel might slip beyond the scheduled date, it now appears that they will be completed on time. The largest remaining contingent is from the United States, which has maintained the biggest troop presence throughout. Several other coalition countries already have pulled out their smaller garrisons, including Poland, which completed its drawdown in March, and Germany , whose soldiers left in August. The departure closes a chapter that began in 2014, when ISIS seized large parts of the country and U.S.-led forces – which had previously invaded and occupied Iraq in 2003 and then withdrawn in 2011 – returned at Baghdad’s invitation. A number of Iraqi armed groups that first formed to combat ISIS came to cast the coalition as a threat. Aligned with Iran, these groups long invoked the coalition’s presence as a justification for keeping weapons and command structures outside the Iraqi state. With coalition forces on their way out, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has declared that these groups must now disarm. But the coalition is leaving amid a Middle East war sparked by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, in which Tehran and some of its aligned groups based in Iraq have launched attacks on U.S. targets in Gulf Arab countries, Jordan and Iraq’s own Kurdistan region. The question is whether Baghdad can and will use the end of this foreign military mission to gain greater control of armed actors who – whatever justification they may offer – have reasons for fighting that extend well beyond opposition to the coalition’s presence. The End of a Mission The U.S.-led Global Coalition to Defeat the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria – dubbed Operation Inherent Resolve by the U.S. military – is ending its mission twelve years after its establishment. At that time, in 2014, a marauding ISIS had capitalised on the instability that gripped much of the Arab world following the 2011 uprisings, helped by the acquisition of conventional weapons from Iraqi and Syrian forces that quickly retreated from major cities such as Mosul and Raqqa in the face of the group’s onslaught. It exploited growing sectarian tensions in Iraq and perceptions of political exclusion among its Sunni Arab population to seize much of the country’s Sunni Arab heartland. In June 2014, ISIS declared a caliphate in Iraq and Syria and at its height, in May 2015, controlled as much as a third of Iraqi territory. Having terminated the U.S. occupation of Iraq only three years earlier, then-U.S. President Barack Obama decided to send troops back to prevent ISIS from expanding further and reverse its gains in both countries. In the ensuing years, the U.S. and dozens of coalition partners supported military operations against the group in both Iraq and Syria at the same time as they sought to help rebuild and train the Iraqi army, which had collapsed in a matter of days after the ISIS offensive. While the Iraqi government declared victory over ISIS as early as December 2017, having retaken Mosul and other key cities from ISIS control and secured its border with Syria, the coalition endured. It remained in the country even after March 2019, when the final ISIS stronghold in Baghouz, Syria fell; that loss marked the end of the group’s control of the last bit of the territory it had grabbed since beginning its 2014 offensive. The coalition – which included sizeable contingents from France, the UK and Türkiye in addition to the U.S. – stayed on for several reasons. First, it continued to support Iraqi armed forces suppressing residual ISIS cells for years after the recapture of Baghouz. The Iraqi army and Kurdish region’s armed forces ( peshmerga ) continued to suffer occasional hit-and-run attacks in the so-called disputed territories, an area claimed by both the federal and regional governments, whose rugged terrain offered ISIS fighters plenty of hideouts. As late as August 2024, U.S. troops operating alongside Iraqi forces sustained injuries during a raid on an ISIS cell in Anbar province. Secondly, the coalition used Iraq as a base from which to conduct operations against the group and others across the border in Syria, where a civil war raged for years, and where the U.S. partnered with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) until April. The ISIS danger appears to have significantly receded. Despite occasional attacks by its remnants, the group has lost its ideological traction. Though some people in both Iraq and Syria continue to harbour the grievances that ISIS played upon to galvanise support, few want to relive the era of the so-called caliphate, which triggered years of conflict and destroyed many of the communities the group ostensibly sought to protect. Moreover, the security gaps that ISIS exploited in 2014 have also narrowed in both countries. Syria’s new authorities have yet to establish full control of the country’s provinces and borders, but the process of integrating the previously autonomous SDF in the north east under the central government’s command is helping secure areas that remain vulnerable to ISIS. In Iraq, state forces are better prepared to repel any domestic or external threat the group might pose. Though the coalition and the Iraqi government share the assessment that Iraqi forces can counter ISIS on their own, the withdrawal is also politically expedient for both Baghdad and Washington. For years, despite its cooperation with coalition forces, Baghdad viewed their presence as a liability, not least because Iran-aligned armed groups seized on it to claim that the U.S. occupation was continuing. Those groups also accused the U.S. of using its foothold in Iraq to monitor Iran and the “axis of resistance” – its partners in the region. This latter charge became a justification for the Iraqi groups to retain their arms and command structures independent from the Iraqi state forces. Domestic political dynamics on the U.S. side may not have been as clear-cut, but they nevertheless militated for withdrawal. Trump was never the pure non-interventionist that he seemed to tout himself as being, but he has long sounded off against the Iraq war (a key theme of his 2016 campaign) and had already considered withdrawing from Syria during his first term. Despite his growing penchant for military intervention in his second term, Trump has continued to inveigh against endless U.S. wars, notably in the Middle East. Departing from Iraq is thus consistent both with the president’s longstanding rhetoric and also the views of significant parts of his political base. To the extent that Washington had contended that the coalition remained in Iraq at its government’s request, Baghdad’s desire for a troop withdrawal has for some time been a complication. Lastly, as a U.S. official noted to Crisis Group, amid the war with Iran, withdrawal would have the added benefit of reducing readily accessible U.S. targets for Tehran. Unlike during the 2011 U.S. withdrawal, Iraqis need not anticipate the next war; it is already affecting the country. In theory, the withdrawal should mark a milestone in Iraq’s relationship with the U.S. and its long road to normalcy following the chaos and violence that have plagued the country since the 2003 U.S. invasion. A series of Iraqi governments have desired to forge bilateral security cooperation agreements on Iraq’s own terms and with countries of its choosing. Baghdad can now strike these deals, not only with the U.S., but also with other former coalition partners such as the UK and France. But however politically necessary it may have deemed the withdrawal, Baghdad will hardly be able to sell the coalition’s departure as a celebratory moment, given that it coincides with the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which has turned Iraq into a battleground. Instead, the withdrawal’s timing will focus further attention on that conflict’s spillover effects. Unlike during the 2011 U.S. withdrawal, Iraqis need not anticipate the next war; it is already affecting the country. The fears of many Iraqis are therefore presently not centred around the risk of a resurgent ISIS but rather around Iran-aligned domestic groups that, in solidarity with their “axis of resistance” partners, and notwithstanding the U.S. withdrawal, may take action in defiance of the government’s policy of neutrality in the U.S.-Iran war, and thereby provoke military retaliation by outside actors. Some of the complications that the withdrawal could present for the Iraqi-U.S. relationship would have been difficult to anticipate when the drawdown timeline was conceived. That happened at another tense moment, following the outbreak of the Gaza war, when U.S. backing for Israel’s brutal military response to Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attacks undermined public support for bilateral close ties. In September 2024, when Zaidi’s predecessor Mohammed Shia’ al-Sudani was prime minister and Joe Biden was U.S. president, Baghdad and Washington agreed on a phased end to the coalition’s military mission. It would start with the coalition’s withdrawal from bases in federal Iraq by September 2025, to be followed by the final withdrawal from the Kurdistan region by the next 30 September. Now, with the U.S.-Iran war as backdrop, the withdrawal may well attract less attention as an indicator of the country’s recovery from ISIS than as a test of whether its government can repair Iraq’s battered sovereignty and protect its internal security at a moment of regional crisis. Reining In Armed Groups Zaidi has declared that the end of the coalition mission should mark the beginning of disarmament for groups that operate independently of the state. He has set June 2027 as the deadline for its completion. His political argument is straightforward: once the coalition troops are gone, the armed factions should no longer be able to invoke their presence as grounds for maintaining separate military structures. As he announces the mission’s conclusion on 30 September, he is expecting some of the factions to welcome a development that meets their longstanding demand and to reciprocate with their own commitment to cease hostilities. But not all of the armed groups will do so, given the variations among them and the dynamics created by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. The Popular Mobilisation Forces, or Hashd al-Shaabi, emerged as a collection of Shiite armed groups assembled to fight ISIS and were subsequently nominally incorporated into Iraq’s formal security apparatus, with many retaining independent chains of command. They do not form a single faction and have very different relationships with Tehran. Not all have engaged in attacks outside Iraq’s borders. Some groups, such as Asaib Ahl al-Haq, appear willing to negotiate their future relationship with the state. Others, including factions associated with the self-described Islamic Resistance in Iraq, such as Kata’ib Hizbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba, are tied ideologically and operationally to Iran’s regional network. Their opposition to the U.S. extends well beyond the presence of coalition troops in Iraq, and they have served as a valuable vector for Iranian power projection. It is these latter factions that have participated in the Middle East war, striking U.S.-linked targets and energy infrastructure in neighbouring countries, including Jordan, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Their actions have strained Baghdad’s relations with Gulf states and, as noted, exposed Iraq to military retaliation by both the U.S. and Saudi Arabia. Zaidi thus has good reasons of his own to want to curb them, as his government cannot credibly reassure its neighbours, attract investment or pursue a foreign policy of neutrality while armed actors make decisions on war and peace independently of its will. Negotiations under way with individual groups offer a possible, albeit incremental, pathway to bringing personnel and capabilities under state command. Negotiations under way with individual groups offer a possible, albeit incremental, pathway to bringing personnel and capabilities under state command. They also are almost certain to take far longer than Zaidi’s deadline allows. If the talks stall, Zaidi could face U.S. pressure to use force against groups that earlier prime ministers were reluctant to confront militarily, fearing an intra-Shiite conflict and friction with Iran. In a mid-September interview , Zaidi said groups continuing to function as separate militias would be considered outlaws. He has yet to specify what action the government would take to corral those that defy him. As long as Tehran relies on close Iraqi partners in its war with the U.S., these groups have reason to preserve their military autonomy and may seek to prolong negotiations without relinquishing their arms. Even after the coalition’s withdrawal, they will likely point to other foreign security relationships, including Türkiye’s garrison in northern Iraq, to defend their stance. Some have also argued that any disarmament plan must simultaneously address the status of the Kurdish region’s peshmerga, although the parallel is inapt: peshmerga forces are governed by a specific law under the Iraqi constitution regarding federal regions’ responsibility to organise their own internal and border security. The government therefore ought to distinguish between forces operating under recognised state or regional authority, and factions conducting attacks without any such justification. The Kurdish Region’s Vulnerabilities The coalition’s departure has particular significance in the Kurdistan region, where its forces have supported the peshmerga and where U.S. troops remained even after leaving other bases in Iraq in September 2025. Erbil is not happy to see them depart. Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani described withdrawal at this moment as “ shameful ”, no doubt because he is concerned about how to manage the threat posed by Iran and Iran-aligned groups, which have systematically targeted the region since the war began in February. Some of the strikes appear to have been motivated by the presence of U.S. forces, in line with attacks on other nearby countries hosting U.S. bases. But the near-daily strikes also have often hit Iraqi-based Iranian Kurdish opposition groups and were described by a Kurdish official to Crisis Group as a warning to Kurdistan to keep those groups out of the current conflict. Certainly, the coalition’s withdrawal will exacerbate vulnerabilities. Coalition forces based in Erbil provided the region with some level of air defence. Their impending departure will mean the loss of those capabilities, further exposing the region to missile and drone attack. The Kurdish official noted to Crisis Group that worries about the withdrawal were “not just about security and protection, but the message this sends to our adversaries”, reflecting fears that Iran and others will see the U.S. drawdown as an indication that they would no longer take a significant interest in the region’s future. Still, U.S. support will not necessarily dry up entirely, even if the basis for it will change. To date, U.S. support for the peshmerga has been governed by a memorandum of understanding between the Pentagon and the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs, first signed in 2016 and last renewed in 2022 . But though the U.S. does not wish to extend the agreement, Kurdish authorities will continue to press Washington and other coalition partners for aid in the form of strikes, intelligence sharing, training and equipment – none of which necessarily requires a troop presence inside Iraq – as well as broader reassurance of assistance in facing the military threat from Iran and the groups that it backs. It may help that the regional government announced in September its completion of a peshmerga reorganisation sought by the U.S. and agreed to in the lapsing memorandum. But future cooperation will require further work to define the terms on which Baghdad, Erbil and foreign partners will operate. Erbil and Baghdad, whose relationship has traditionally been fraught, will surely have to work together more closely. That said, at least for now, Kurdish officials say they are impressed with Zaidi and believe he is sincere in his stated intention of trying to tackle the militia problem. Looking Ahead When Trump returned to the White House for his second term, much of his base hoped and believed that his administration would avoid military adventurism and seek to extract the country from strategic quagmires. Some of his personnel decisions, particularly at the Pentagon, seemed to lend credence to such speculation, as did the foreign policy views of his vice president, JD Vance. Officials who sought to pursue a more restraint-oriented foreign policy or to concentrate on competition with China by downsizing other overseas commitments were not a dominant force within the new administration but nevertheless held key positions. Both of these groups favoured reassessing U.S. force posture in the Middle East, particularly the legacy missions in both Iraq and Syria. Whatever influence these camps have, their perspectives have not guided key foreign policy decisions in Trump’s latest year in office, which has been characterised by aggressive unilateralism and reliance on military force as a tool of statecraft. But the trajectory of U.S. policy on Iraq and Syria is an exception to that trend. Administration sources tell Crisis Group that, buoyed by the unexpected ouster of President Bashar al-Assad in Syria, key U.S. officials, particularly at the Pentagon, pushed to reassess the U.S. troop presence there and prevailed in a series of internal policy debates on the matter. Those efforts were boosted when it became clear how vulnerable U.S. troops in the region had become as a result of the conflict with Iran. U.S. officials also have positive views of Zaidi, who visited Washington in July and was received warmly by Trump. They are particularly pleased by Zaidi’s pledges on armed group disarmament. Even those who are sceptical of how those efforts will fare appreciate the Iraqi prime minister’s tone and confidence. What comes next for U.S.-Iraq relations will likely depend on the uncertain trajectory of the U.S. war with Iran. What comes next for U.S.-Iraq relations will likely depend on the uncertain trajectory of the U.S. war with Iran. A prolonged conflict is likely to lead Iran to enlist its partners in Iraq to use the country as a staging ground for significant attacks on the interests of the U.S. and its regional partners. That in turn would inevitably undermine the bilateral relationship and could trigger retaliatory U.S. moves at a time when Washington still enjoys outsized influence, including because it controls a significant portion of Iraq’s oil proceeds, which are deposited in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The Trump administration has already twice used the leverage the oil revenue affords the U.S. in pressing Iraq to take more proactive measures to dilute Iran’s influence. For now, Zaidi’s ascension has eased strains, and the U.S. withdrawal gives him an argument for reining in armed groups. That may be enough for him to make progress with some of the groups, but doubters are right to question how far he will be able to go. Indeed, it would be entirely unrealistic to expect that Baghdad can compel the surrender of weapons or severing of ties with Iran forged through years of regional conflict. The symbolism of 30 September is significant, but in the end Iraq’s stability will depend more on whether the U.S. gives it the time and space required to bring armed groups under its central authority, and whether Baghdad and Washington work together to protect Iraq from the worst effects of the U.S.-Iranian confrontation in the meantime.
